parole.significato: The act or process of compiling or gathering together from various sources.
parole.testo: English compile + -ation, from Middle French, from Latin compilatio (“a raking together, a plundering, a collection of documents”).

parole.significato: to convince
parole.testo: From Middle French complaire, from Latin complaceō.

parole.significato: The act or process of complicating.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French complication, from Latin complicatio, complicationem. Morphologically complicate + -ion.

parole.significato: A plot (involving more than one person), conspiracy
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French complot (“crowd-, plot”).

parole.significato: The manner in which one behaves or conducts oneself.
parole.testo: From Late Middle French comportement. By surface analysis, comport + -ment.

parole.significato: Made up of multiple components; compound or complex.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French composite, from Latin compositus, past participle of compōnō (“put together”). Doublet of compost, compote, and kompot.

parole.significato: Compost, composted manure.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French composture (“compost”), from late Old French composture, possibly from Latin compositūra, compostūra (“composition”); equivalent to compost + -ure. Compare Portuguese compostura, Spanish compostura.

parole.significato: Composed of elements; not simple.
parole.testo: From Middle English compounen, from Middle French componre, compondre (“to put together”), from Latin componō, from Latin com- (“together”) + ponō (“to put”).

parole.significato: A thorough understanding.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French compréhension, from Latin comprehēnsiō (“taking together”), from com- (“with, together”) + prehendō (“take”).

parole.significato: Broadly or completely covering; including a large proportion of something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from late Middle French compréhensif, from Late Latin comprehēnsīvus, from Latin comprehendō.

parole.significato: A multiply folded piece of cloth, a pouch of ice, etc., used to apply to a patient's skin, cover the dressing of wounds…
parole.testo: From Middle French compresse, from compresse (“to compress”), from Late Latin compressare (“to press hard/together”), from Latin compressus, the past participle of comprimō (“to compress”), itself from com- (“together”) + premō (“press”).

parole.significato: An increase in density; the act of compressing, or the state of being compressed; compaction.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French compression, from Latin compressiō, equivalent to compress + -ion.

parole.significato: The settlement of differences by arbitration or by consent reached by mutual concessions.
parole.testo: From Middle French compromis, from Medieval Latin, Late Latin compromissum (“a compromise, originally a mutual promise to refer to arbitration”), prop. neuter of Latin compromissus, past participle of compromittere (“to make a mutual promise to abide by the decision of an arbiter”), from com- (“toge

parole.significato: An irrational need or irresistible urge to perform some action, often despite negative consequences.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French compulsion, from Late Latin compulsiō, from Latin compellere (“to compel, coerce”); see compel.

parole.significato: The act or process of computing; calculation; reckoning.
parole.testo: From late Middle English computacioun, from Middle French computation, from Latin computatiō, from computare (“sum up, reckon, compute”); see compute. Morphologically compute + -ation.

parole.significato: A mate, companion, or associate.
parole.testo: From earlier cumrade, camrade, comerade, camerade, camarade, from Middle French camarade, from Spanish camarada or Italian camerata (“chamber mate”), from Medieval Latin *camarata, from Latin camara, camera (“vaulted room, chamber”); see chamber. Compare camaraderie and chamberlain.

parole.significato: Having a common center.
parole.testo: From Middle English concentrik, from Middle French concentrique, from Medieval Latin concentricus, from Latin con- (“with, together”) + centrum (“circle, center”). Equivalent to con- + -centric. By surface analysis, con- + centre + -ic.

parole.significato: An abstract and general idea; an abstraction.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French concept, from Latin conceptus (“a thought, purpose, also a conceiving, etc.”), from concipiō (“to take in, conceive”). Doublet of conceit and concetto. See conceive.

parole.significato: That which affects one’s welfare or happiness. A matter of interest to someone.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French concerner, from Medieval Latin concernō, concernere (“I distinguish, have respect to”), from Latin concernō (“to mix, sift, or mingle together, as in a sieve”), combined form of con- + cernō (“distinguish”).

parole.significato: The act of conceding.
parole.testo: From late Middle English concession, from Middle French concession, from Latin concessiō (“a grant, permission, conceding”), from concēdō. Doublet of concessio.

parole.significato: The process of bringing peace and harmony; the ending of strife.
parole.testo: From Middle French conciliation.

parole.significato: The set of apartments in which cardinals are secluded while the process to elect a pope takes place.
parole.testo: PIE word  *ḱóm The noun is derived from Late Middle English conclave (“private chamber; (Roman Catholicism) private room where election of the Pope takes place; meeting held for this purpose”), borrowed from Middle French conclave (modern French conclave), or directly from its etymon Latin conclāve

parole.significato: Accompanying; conjoining; attending; concurrent.
parole.testo: First attested 1607; from Middle French concomitant, from Latin concomitāns, the present participle of concomitor (“to accompany”), from con- (“together”) + comitor (“to accompany”), from comes (“companion”).

parole.significato: A large open space in or in front of a building where people can gather, particularly one joining various paths, as in…
parole.testo: From Middle English concours, from Middle French concours and its etymon Latin concursus, concursum, from concurrere (“to run together”). See concur. Doublet of concours.

parole.significato: Greatly to be desired or lusted after; exciting concupiscence.
parole.testo: From Middle English concupiscibill, concupiscibl, concupiscible, concupyscyble, concupyssible, from Middle French concupiscible and its etymon, Latin concupīscibilis.

parole.significato: To concentrate toward the essence by making more close, compact, or dense, thereby decreasing size or volume.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French condenser, from Latin condēnsō.

parole.significato: One who conducts or leads; a guide; a director.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French conductour, from Old French conduitor, from Latin conductor.

parole.significato: A union or alliance of states or political organizations.
parole.testo: From Middle English confederacion, confideracion and Middle French confédération, from Old French confederacion, from Latin cōnfoederātiō. Doublet of confederacy.

parole.significato: To grant as a possession; to bestow.
parole.testo: From Early Modern English conferre, from Middle French conférer, from Old French conferer, from Latin cōnferō. Compare Dutch confereren, German konferieren, Danish konferere, Swedish konferera. Doublet of collate. See also infer, relate and refer, delate and defer, as well as prelate and prefer amon

parole.significato: The act of consulting together formally; serious conversation or discussion; interchange of views.
parole.testo: From Middle French conférence, from Medieval Latin cōnferentia, from Latin cōnferēns, omitting several steps, from con- + ferō. Compare parallel Russian собра́ние (sobránije), Russian сбо́рище (sbórišče), akin to с- (s-), со- (so-) + брать (bratʹ), ultimately from the same Indo-European prefix and r

parole.significato: Very sure of something; positive.
parole.testo: From Middle French confident, from Latin confidens (“confident, i.e. self-confident, in a good or bad sense, bold, daring, audacious, impudent”), present participle of confidere (“to trust fully, confide”). See confide.

parole.significato: The form of a thing, as depending on the relative placement of the parts of a thing's shape.
parole.testo: From Middle French configuration, from Latin cōnfigūrātiō. Morphologically configure + -ation.

parole.significato: To have a common boundary with; to border on.
parole.testo: From Middle French confiner, from confins, from Medieval Latin confines, from Latin confinium, from confīnis.

parole.significato: A large fire extending to many objects, or over a large space; a general burning.
parole.testo: From Middle French, from Latin cōnflagrātiō (“burning, conflagration”).

parole.significato: To adapt to something by more closely matching it, especially something normative.
parole.testo: From Middle English conformen, borrowed from Middle French and Anglo-Norman conformer, from Latin conformāre (“to mould, to shape after”).

parole.significato: The state of things being similar or identical.
parole.testo: From Middle English conformyte, from Middle French conformité. By surface analysis, conform + -ity.

parole.significato: A group with a common interest.
parole.testo: From Middle French confraternité.

parole.significato: To stand or meet facing, especially in competition, hostility or defiance; to come face to face with.
parole.testo: From Middle French confronter, borrowed from Medieval Latin cōnfrontāre, from con- + frontem (“front, forehead”).

parole.significato: The act of confronting or challenging another, especially face to face.
parole.testo: From Middle French. Morphologically confront + -ation.

parole.significato: To show (something or someone) to be false or wrong; to disprove or refute.
parole.testo: From Middle French confuter, from Latin confūtō.

parole.significato: The act or process of passing, or causing to pass, from a fluid to a solid state, as by the abstraction of heat; the ac…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French congelation (compare modern congélation), from Latin congelatio, congelationem, from congelo.

parole.significato: The act of congratulating.
parole.testo: From Middle English congratulacion, from Middle French congratulation or its etymon Latin congrātulātiō, from congrātulor (“to congratulate”). By surface analysis, congratulate + -ion.

parole.significato: joined together; combined; joint
parole.testo: From Middle French. Doublet of conjunct.

parole.significato: Of or relating to marriage, or the relationship of spouses; connubial.
parole.testo: From Middle French conjugal, from Latin coniugālis (“con- + iugum ('yoke')”).

parole.significato: Conjuring, legerdemain or magic.
parole.testo: From Middle English conjuracioun, from Middle French conjuration, from Old French conjuracion, from Latin coniuratio (“a swearing together, a conspiracy”).

parole.significato: A state of connection; connectedness.
parole.testo: From Middle French connexité.

parole.significato: To conquer.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English conquesten, borrowed from Middle French conquester, from Old French conquester.

parole.significato: Synonym of conqueror
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French conquesteur. By surface analysis, conquest (“to conquer”) + -or.

parole.significato: A consanguineous or family relationship through parentage or descent.
parole.testo: From Middle English consanguinite, consanguinyte, consanguinytee, consanguynyte, consangwinyte, from Middle French consanguinéité, consanguinité (from Old French consanguinité) and its etymon Latin cōnsanguinitās (accusative cōnsanguinitātem), from cōnsanguineus + -itās, from Latin com- (“together”)

parole.significato: Thorough, careful, or vigilant in one’s task performance; painstaking.
parole.testo: From Middle French conscientieux, from Medieval Latin cōnscientiōsus. Its English equivalent could possibly be analyzed as conscient + -ous. See more at conscience.

parole.significato: Involuntary labor, especially military service, demanded by some established authority.
parole.testo: From Middle French conscription, from Latin cōnscriptiō (“levying of troops”).

parole.significato: Following as a result, inference, or natural effect.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French conséquent, from Latin consequens, consequentem, present participle of consequi (“to follow”), from con- + sequi (“to follow”). Compare French conséquent.

parole.significato: A person who favors maintenance of the status quo.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French conservatif, from Latin cōnservō (“to preserve”). Equivalent to conserve + -ative.

parole.significato: To think about seriously.
parole.testo: From Middle English consideren, from Middle French considerer, from Latin considerare.

parole.significato: To transfer to the custody of, usually for sale, transport, or safekeeping.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French consigner or directly from Latin cōnsignō (“furnish with a seal”), from con- + signō (“mark, sign”).

parole.significato: To be.
parole.testo: From Middle French consister, from Latin consistō (“stand together, stop, become hard or solid, agree with, continue, exist”), from com- (“together”) + sistō (“to cause to stand, stand”).

parole.significato: Logical consistency; lack of self-contradiction.
parole.testo: From Middle French. Compare French consistance. By surface analysis, consist + -ence.

parole.significato: A form of rhyme having the same consonants but different vowels.
parole.testo: From Middle English consonance, from Middle French consonance, from Latin cōnsonantia. Doublet of consonancy. By surface analysis, con- + son- + -ance.

parole.significato: The spouse of a monarch.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French, ultimately from Latin cōnsors. As “companion or partner”, via Middle English consorte.

parole.significato: Agreement or concurrence for some end or purpose.
parole.testo: From Middle English conspiracioun, from Middle French conspiration, from Latin cōnspīrātiō, cōnspīrātiōnem. Doublet of conspiracy.

parole.significato: Custom, familiarity.
parole.testo: From Middle English consuetude, from Middle French consuetude, from Old French consuetude, learnedly borrowed from Latin cōnsuētūdō. Doublet of costume, custom, and kastom.

parole.significato: A visit to consult somebody, such as a doctor; a consultation.
parole.testo: From Middle French consulter, from Latin cōnsultum, from cōnsultus, from cōnsulō.

parole.significato: The act of consulting.
parole.testo: From Middle French consultation, from Latin consultatio. Morphologically consult + -ation.

parole.significato: That which is held together with another thing.
parole.testo: From Middle French contenement.

parole.significato: Marked by heated arguments or controversy.
parole.testo: From Middle French contentieux, from Latin contentiōsus (“quarrelsome, perverse”), from contentiō (“contention”), from contendere, past participle contentus (“to contend”). Equivalent to English contention + -ous.

parole.significato: The state or degree of being contented or satisfied.
parole.testo: From Middle French contentement. By surface analysis, content + -ment.

parole.significato: A weaving together of parts.
parole.testo: From Middle French contexture, from contexte + -ure after texture.

parole.significato: Lack of interruption or disconnection; the quality of being continuous in space or time.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French continuité, from Latin continuitas. By surface analysis, continu(e) + -ity.

parole.significato: The act or result of contorting; the state of being contorted: the twisting of something, especially oneself.
parole.testo: Derived from Middle French contortion, from Latin contortiō.

parole.significato: To draw together or nearer; to shorten, narrow, or lessen.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Middle French contracter, from Latin contractum, past participle of contrahere (“to bring together, to bring about, to conclude a bargain”), from con- (“with, together”) + trahere (“to draw, to pull”). The verb developed after the noun, and originally meant only "draw toget

parole.significato: Opposition or contrariness; cross-purposes, marked contrast.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French contrariété, from Late Latin contrarietas, from contrarius, from Latin contra (“against”). By surface analysis, contrary + -ety.

parole.significato: To act contrary to an order; to fail to conform to a regulation or obligation.
parole.testo: From Middle French contravenir (French contrevenir), from Latin contraveniō.

parole.significato: The act of contravening (a rule, regulation, law, or order) or of not fulfilling (an obligation, promise, or agreement).
parole.testo: From Middle French contravention.

parole.significato: Controversy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French controverse.

parole.significato: controversy
parole.testo: From Middle French controversion and its etymon Latin contrōversiō.

parole.significato: Synonym of bruise.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French contusion, from Latin contūsiōnem, accusative singular of contūsiō, from contūsus, past participle of contundō (“to beat”), by surface analysis, com- + tundō.

parole.significato: A gradual healing after illness or injury.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French convalescence, from Late Latin convalēscentia (“regaining of health”), from Latin convalēscēn(t-)s, present participle of convalēscere (“to become strong or well”); see convalesce.

parole.significato: To come together; to meet; to unite.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French convenir, from Latin convenio, convenire (“come together”), from con- (“with, together”) + veniō (“come”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷm̥yéti, from the root *gʷem-.

parole.significato: A meeting or gathering.
parole.testo: Recorded since about 1440, borrowed from Middle French convention, from Latin conventiō (“meeting, assembling; agreement, convention”), from conveniō (“come, gather or meet together, assemble”), from con- (“with, together”) + veniō (“come”). Equivalent to convene + -tion.

parole.significato: Curved or bowed outward like the outside of a bowl, circle, or sphere.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French convexe, from Latin convexus (“arched”).

parole.significato: To convene, to cause to assemble for a meeting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French convoquer, from Latin convocare, from con- (“with”) + vocō (“to call”). Doublet of convocate.

parole.significato: The act of coordinating, making different people or things work together for a goal or effect.
parole.testo: From Middle French coordination, from Late Latin coōrdinātiōnem (accusative of coōrdinātiō), from con- + ōrdinātiō. Morphologically coordinate + -ion.

parole.significato: Synonym of copiousness.
parole.testo: From Middle French copiosité or Late Latin cōpiōsitās. By surface analysis, copi(ous) + -osity.

parole.significato: The act of coupling or joining; union; conjunction.
parole.testo: From Middle French copulation, from Latin copulo (“to join, unite, connect”).

parole.significato: A raven or crow (typically Corvus corax).
parole.testo: From Middle French corbeau, from Old French corb (from Latin corvus (“raven”)) or Old French corbel (“crow”) (from Late Latin corbellus, from Latin corvus). See also Norman corbin.

parole.significato: A ribbon normally worn diagonally across the chest as a decoration or insignia of rank etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English cordon, from Middle French cordon, from Old French cordon, diminutive of corde. More at cord.

parole.significato: Any tree or shrub of the dogwood subgenera, Cornus subg. Arctocrania (syn. Cornus subg. Chamaepericlymenum) or Cornus s…
parole.testo: From Middle English corneille, borrowed from Middle French corneille, from Vulgar Latin *cornicula, from Latin cornus (“the European cornel”).

parole.significato: The white headdress worn by the Sisters of Charity.
parole.testo: From Middle French cornette, diminutive of corne, from Latin cornua (“horns”).

parole.significato: A small crown, such as is worn by a noble.
parole.testo: From Middle French couronnette, from Old French coronete, diminutive of corone (“crown”), from Latin corona, from Ancient Greek κορώνη (korṓnē, “a type of sea-bird, perhaps shearwater; a crow; anything curved or hooked (like a door handle or the tip of a bow); a type of crown”).

parole.significato: A reciprocal, parallel or complementary relationship between two or more comparable objects.
parole.testo: From Middle French corrélation. Morphologically correlate + -ion.

parole.significato: To be equivalent or similar in character, quantity, quality, origin, structure, function etc.
parole.testo: From Middle French correspondre, from Latin com- (“with”) + respondeo (“to match, to answer to”), equivalent to co- + respond.

parole.significato: A fellow rival; a competitor; a rival.
parole.testo: From Middle French corrival, from Latin corrīvālis.

parole.significato: A member or descendant of an originally (semi-)nomadic population of Eastern Europe and the adjacent parts of Asia, for…
parole.testo: From Middle French cosaque, from Middle Polish Kozak, from Middle Ukrainian коза́къ (kozák), from Kipchak *qazaq (whence Armeno-Kipchak խազախ (xazax)), from Old Turkic 𐰴𐰔𐰍𐰸 (*qazǧaq, “profiteer”), from 𐰴𐰔𐰍𐰣𐰢𐰴 (qazǧanmaq, “to acquire”), from 𐰴𐰔𐰢𐰴 (qazmaq, “to dig out”), from Proto-Turkic *kaŕ-. Doubl

parole.significato: Constipated.
parole.testo: From Middle French costivé, past participle of costiver (“to constipate”), ultimately from Latin cōnstīpātus (“constipated”). Doublet of constipate.

parole.significato: To go side by side with; hence, to pass by; to outrun and get before.
parole.testo: Probably related to French côté (“side”) via Middle French costé.

parole.significato: A diminutive of the bendlet, containing one half its area or one quarter the area of the bend: a thin line borne around…
parole.testo: From Middle French cotice, costice, from côte + -ice, from Latin costa (“rib”).

parole.significato: Lying with belly down and front legs extended; crouching.
parole.testo: From Middle English couchant, from Middle French couchant.

parole.significato: To give and receive; C; to exchange.
parole.testo: From Middle French contrechange (noun), contrechanger (verb).

parole.significato: A buttress built against a wall.
parole.testo: From Middle French contrefort.

parole.significato: A melody added to an existing one, especially one added to provide harmony whilst each retains its simultaneous identit…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English [Term?], from Middle French contrepoint, from Medieval Latin contrāpūnctum. Equivalent to counter- + point.

parole.significato: A second signature added to a document to affirm the validity of the signature of the first person.
parole.testo: From Middle French contresigne. Equivalent to counter- + sign.

parole.significato: Any of a family of old French dances from the late Renaissance and the Baroque era in triple metre.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French courante.

parole.significato: To bend; to bow.
parole.testo: From Middle English courben, from Middle French courber, from Latin curvō. Doublet of curb.

parole.significato: A female prostitute, especially one with high-status or wealthy clients.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French courtisane, from Italian cortigiana, feminine of cortigiano (“courtier”), from corte (“court”), itself from Latin cohors.

parole.significato: A hard, crisp or crunchy cake or biscuit.
parole.testo: From Middle English crakenelle, craknel, krakenelle, apparently an alteration of Middle French craquelin.

parole.significato: The husk of grain; chaff.
parole.testo: From Middle English crappe, also in plural: crappys, craps (“chaff; buckwheat”), from Middle French crape, from Old French crappe, crapin (“chaff”) (compare Medieval Latin crappa pl, also crapinum), from Old Dutch krappen (“to cut off, pluck off”) (whence Middle Dutch crappe, crap (“a chop, cutlet”)

parole.significato: Believable or plausible.
parole.testo: From Middle English credible, borrowed from Middle French credible, from Latin crēdibilis (“worthy of belief”), from crēdō (“believe”); see credit.

parole.significato: To believe; to put credence in.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French crédit (“belief, trust”), from Latin crēditum (“a loan, credit”), neuter of crēditus, past participle of crēdere (“to believe”). The verb is from the noun. Doublet of shraddha, creed.

parole.significato: A willingness to believe in someone or something in the absence of reasonable proof; credulousness.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English credulite (“faith, belief”), borrowed from Middle French credulité (French crédulité), from Latin crēdulitās. Corresponding to credulous + -ity (compare credulosity).

parole.significato: Twilight.
parole.testo: From Middle French crepuscule m, ultimately from Latin crepusculum n. Doublet of crepuscle and crepusculum.

parole.significato: Hair of the head.
parole.testo: From Middle French crine (whence also French crin), Italian crine, or directly from Latin crīnis (“hair of the head, lock of hair, plume”).

parole.significato: Each of the small hair-like feathers growing around a hawk's cere.
parole.testo: Probably from Middle French crin (“hair”) + -et.

parole.significato: Protective armor for a horse's neck.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French criniere.

parole.significato: To criticise.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French critique, from Latin criticus, from Ancient Greek κριτικός (kritikós, “of or for judging, able to discern”), from κρίνω (krínō, “to judge”).

parole.significato: A little bud or knob at the top of a deer's antler, or as the predevelopmental stage of the antler.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French croche, equivalent to English crochet (“hook”), croc (“hook”), from Frankish *krok (“hook”), from Proto-Germanic *krukaz, *krōkaz (“something bent, hook”), from Proto-Indo-European *ger- (“to turn, bend, wind”). Cognate with Old Norse krókr (“hook”).

parole.significato: A coronet, small crown.
parole.testo: From Middle English crovnette, crownet, from Middle French [Term?].

parole.significato: The state of being crude.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French crudité, from Latin crūditās. By surface analysis, crude + -ity. Doublet of crudité.

parole.significato: Used in the names of units of volume formed by multiplying a unit of length by itself twice.
parole.testo: From Middle French cubique, equivalent to cube + -ic.

parole.significato: Any member of the family Cucurbitaceae of gourds.
parole.testo: From Middle English cocurbite, concurbite, cucurbita, cucurbite, from Middle French cucurbite and Latin cucurbita. Doublet of gourd.

parole.significato: A component of armor, consisting of overlapping plates designed to protect the buttocks.
parole.testo: From Middle French culet, diminutive of cul (“bottom”), from Latin culus (“arse”).

parole.significato: The degree of one's blameworthiness in the commission of a crime or offence.
parole.testo: From Middle French culpabilité.

parole.significato: to maintain in an environment suitable for growth (especially of bacteria) (compare cultivate)
parole.testo: From Middle French culture (“cultivation; culture”), from Latin cultūra (“cultivation; culture”), from cultus, perfect passive participle of colō (“till, cultivate, to grow, worship”) (related to colōnus and colōnia), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷel- (“to move; to turn (around)”).

parole.significato: Possessing the ability to cure, to heal or treat illness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French curatif.

parole.significato: A concrete margin along the edge of a road; a kerb (UK, Australia, New Zealand).
parole.testo: From Middle French courbe (“curve, curved object”), from Latin curvus (“bent, crooked, curved”). Doublet of curve.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a court; courtly.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French curial, from Latin cūriālis.

parole.significato: Running; flowing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French cursif, from Medieval Latin cursīvus, from Latin cursus.

parole.significato: Hasty or superficial.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French cursoire (“rapid”), from Latin cursorius (“hasty, of a race or running”).

parole.significato: A short sword with a curved blade, and a convex edge; once used by sailors when boarding an enemy ship.
parole.testo: From Middle French coutelas, from Old French coutel (“knife”) + -as (augmentative suffix).

parole.significato: A surface created by projecting a closed two-dimensional curve along an axis intersecting the plane of the curve.
parole.testo: From Middle French chilindre, cylindre, from Latin cylindrus, from Ancient Greek κύλινδρος (kúlindros), from κυλίνδω (kulíndō) "I roll or wallow" (intransitive). Doublet of calander and calender.

parole.significato: A person whose outlook is scornfully negative.
parole.testo: From Middle English cynike, cynicke, from Middle French cynique, from Latin cynicus, from Ancient Greek κυνικός (kunikós), originally derived from the portico in Athens called Κυνόσαργες (Kunósarges), the earliest home of the Cynic school, later reinterpreted as being derived from κύων (kúōn, “dog”)

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a cyst.
parole.testo: From Middle French cystique, from Ancient Greek κύστις (kústis).

parole.significato: A long wide-sleeved tunic, which serves as a liturgical vestment in the Roman Catholic and Anglican Churches and is wor…
parole.testo: From Middle French dalmatique, from Ecclesiastical Latin, derived ultimately from the name of the province of Dalmatia.

parole.significato: The eldest son of the king of France. Under the Valois and Bourbon dynasties, the Dauphin of France, generally shortene…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Dauphin, from Middle French dauphin, from Old French dalphin, from Latin delphīnus, from Ancient Greek δελφίς (delphís); the modern pronunciation is sometimes remodelled on Modern French. Doublet of dolphin.

parole.significato: An individual act of debauchery.
parole.testo: 1590s, from Middle French desbaucher (“entice from work or duty”), from Old French desbauchier (“to lead astray”), from des- + bauch (“beam”), from Frankish *balkō, from Proto-Germanic *balkô, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵ- (“beam, plank”); latter origin of balk. Evolution of sense unclear; may be

parole.significato: Weak; feeble.
parole.testo: From Middle French débile (“weak”), from Latin dēbilis.

parole.significato: The act or process of debilitating, or the condition of one who is debilitated; weakness.
parole.testo: From Middle French débilitation.

parole.significato: In bookkeeping, an entry in the left hand column of an account.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French debet, from Latin debitum (“what is owed, a debt”), neuter of debitus, past participle of debere (“to owe”); Doublet of debt.

parole.significato: Any set of rules that have the weight of authority
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French Décalogue, from Latin decalogus, from Ancient Greek δεκάλογος (dekálogos, from δέκα (déka, “ten”) + λόγος (lógos, “statement”)). Equivalent to deca- + -logue.

parole.significato: Appropriate; suitable for the circumstances.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French décent, or its source, Latin decēns, present participle of decet (“it is fitting or suitable”), from Proto-Indo-European *deḱ- (“to take, accept, to receive, greet, be suitable”) (compare Ancient Greek δοκέω (dokéō, “to appear, seem, think”), δέχομαι (dékhomai, “to accept

parole.significato: Likely or attempting to deceive.
parole.testo: From Middle French déceptif, from Latin dēceptīvus, from dēcipiō (“to deceive”).

parole.significato: The act of deciding.
parole.testo: Derived from Middle French, from Latin dēcīsiō, dēcīsiōnis, from dēcīdō (“to decide”).

parole.significato: Having the power or quality of deciding a question or controversy; putting an end to contest or controversy; final; con…
parole.testo: From Middle French décisif, equivalent to decide + -ive.

parole.significato: To recite, e.g., poetry, in a theatrical way; to speak for rhetorical display; to speak pompously, noisily, or theatric…
parole.testo: From Middle French declamer, from Latin dēclāmō.

parole.significato: Serving to declare; having the quality of a declaration.
parole.testo: Derived from Middle French déclaratif.

parole.significato: A falling off, decay or descent.
parole.testo: From late Middle English declinson, from Middle French declinaison (Modern French: déclinaison), from Latin dēclīnātiō. Doublet of declination.

parole.significato: At a given point, the angle between magnetic north and true north.
parole.testo: From Middle English declinacioun, borrowed from Middle French declination, from Latin declinatio. Doublet of declension.

parole.significato: To separate or break down (something) into its components.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French décomposer. Equivalent to de- + compose.

parole.significato: To unlink; to take apart or come apart.
parole.testo: From Middle French découpler. By surface analysis, de- + couple.

parole.significato: Weakened or worn out from age or wear.
parole.testo: From Middle English decrepyt (ante 1439), from Middle French décrépit, from Latin dēcrepitus (“very old”), from crepō (“to creak”).

parole.significato: The state of being decrepit or worn out from age or long use.
parole.testo: From Middle French décrépitude, from Old French, from Latin dēcrepitūdō (“decrepitude”).

parole.significato: Decrepitude.
parole.testo: From Middle French décrépité, from Latin dēcrepitās.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a decree.
parole.testo: From Middle French decretal, from Late Latin dēcrētālis, from Latin decretum.

parole.significato: To decrease, wane.
parole.testo: From Middle French decreu, past participle of decreistre (“to decrease”). Compare accrue.

parole.significato: To denounce as harmful.
parole.testo: C. 1600, from Middle French decrier (“to denigrate; depreciate”), from Old French descrier (“to shout”) (modern décrier). Doublet of descry. The pejorative meaning had not been present in the Middle English loan, but it was present in the French word from at least the 13th century, with a meaning of

parole.significato: Tenfold.
parole.testo: From Middle English decuple, from Middle French décuple, from Late Latin decuplus (“tenfold”), from Latin decem (“ten”), and plicō (“fold”).

parole.significato: That which is deducted; that which is subtracted or removed.
parole.testo: From Middle French déduction, from Latin deductio. Equivalent to deduct + -ion or deduce + -tion.

parole.significato: To reduce by deducting a part, especially when used in a financial sense.
parole.testo: From Middle French défalquer.

parole.significato: Damaging to someone's reputation, especially if untrue.
parole.testo: From Middle French diffamatoire (altered after the prefix de-), from Medieval Latin diffāmātōrius.

parole.significato: Intended for defence; protective.
parole.testo: From Middle French défensif. Morphologically defense + -ive.

parole.significato: To submit to the opinion or desire of others in respect to their judgment or authority.
parole.testo: From late Middle English differren (“to refer for judgement”), from Middle French déférer, from Latin dēferō. Doublet of delate. See also infer, collate and confer, relate and refer, as well as prelate and prefer among others.

parole.significato: A duct in the body serving to carry away from, as opposed to an afferent one.
parole.testo: From Middle English defferent, from Middle French deferent (modern French déférent) or its etymon Latin dēferēns, dēferentis.

parole.significato: A statement of the meaning of a word, word group, sign, or symbol; especially, a dictionary definition.
parole.testo: From Middle English diffinicioun, from Middle French definition, from Latin dēfīnītiō, from dēfīniō. Equivalent to define + -ition.

parole.significato: Explicitly defined.
parole.testo: From Middle French définitif.

parole.significato: Having an unusual and unattractive shape; deformed, misshapen; hence, hideous, ugly.
parole.testo: From Middle English deforme (“out of shape, deformed”) [and other forms], from Middle French deforme (modern French difforme (“misshapen, deformed”)), or directly from its etymon Latin dēfōrmis (“departing physically from the correct shape, deformed, malformed, misshapen, ugly; (figuratively) depart

parole.significato: The state of being deformed.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English deformite, from Middle French deformite, from Latin dēfōrmitās (“deformity, ugliness”), from dēfōrmis (“deformed, ugly”) + -itās, from dē + fōrma (“shape, form”).

parole.significato: To pay or discharge (a debt, expense etc.); to meet (the cost of something).
parole.testo: From Middle French desfrayer, French défrayer, from dé- + Old French fraier (“to spend”).

parole.significato: To lower in value or social position.
parole.testo: From Middle French dégrader.

parole.significato: divine; of or relating to a deity or deities.
parole.testo: From Middle French déifique, from Latin deificus, from deus (“god”) + facio (“to make”).

parole.significato: The act of deifying; exaltation to divine honors; apotheosis.
parole.testo: From Middle English deificacion, from Middle French deifier + -acion or borrowed directly from Latin deificātiō(n), from deific(ā) (“deify”) + -tiō(n) (noun suffix), from de(i) (“god”) + -ficō (“make”). By surface analysis, deif(y) + -ication. * In the Christian, theological sense, influenced by the

parole.significato: Synonym of divinity: the state, position, or fact of being a god.
parole.testo: From Middle French deité, from Latin deitās.

parole.significato: The quality of being delectable.
parole.testo: From Middle English dilectabilites pl, from Middle French delectableté.

parole.significato: Highly pleasing; delightful, especially to any of the senses; delicious.
parole.testo: From Middle English delectable, from Middle French délectable, from Old French delectable, from Medieval Latin delectare (“to delight”). By surface analysis, delect + -able. Piecewise doublet of delightable.

parole.significato: That deliberates, considers carefully.
parole.testo: From Middle French délibératif, from Latin deliberativus.

parole.significato: Synonym of delicacy.
parole.testo: Apparently from Middle French delicatesse, from delicat (“delicate”) + -esse (“quality”), probably after Italian delicatezza. By surface analysis, delicate + -esse.

parole.significato: quality of being delicious
parole.testo: From Middle English delicissite, deliciouste, deliciuste, diliciousite (“delightfulness; of food: deliciousness; a luxury”), from Middle French delicieuseté (compare Medieval Latin dēliciōsitās) or formed within English from delicious + -osity.

parole.significato: Late or failing to pay a debt or other financial obligation, like a mortgage or loan.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French délinquant, ultimately from Latin delinquens, present participle of delinquo.

parole.significato: A political orator or leader, especially in a democratic system, who gains favor by pandering to or exciting the passio…
parole.testo: From Middle French démagogue, from Ancient Greek δημαγωγός (dēmagōgós, “popular leader, mob leader”), from δῆμος (dêmos, “people”) + ἀγωγός (agōgós, “guide”). By surface analysis, dem- + -agogue.

parole.significato: The conveyance or transfer of an estate, either in fee for life or for years, most commonly the latter.
parole.testo: From Middle English demyse, dimise, dimisse, dymyse, from Middle French démise, the feminine singular past participle of démettre (“to put down, relinquish”); from Latin dēmissa, feminine singular of perfect passive participle of dēmittō. The "death" and "end" senses derive by way of euphemism from

parole.significato: Rule by the people, especially as a form of government, such as
parole.testo: From Middle French democratie (French démocratie), from Medieval Latin dēmocratia, from Ancient Greek δημοκρᾰτῐ́ᾱ (dēmokrătĭ́ā). By surface analysis, demo- (“people”) + -cracy (“rule”).

parole.significato: To destroy (buildings, etc.), especially in a planned or intentional fashion.
parole.testo: Attested since the 16th century; from Middle French demoliss-, the stem of some conjugated forms of the verb demolir (“to destroy”, “to tear down”), from Latin dēmōlior (“to tear down”). Displaced native Old English tōweorpan (literally “to throw apart”).

parole.significato: That serves to demonstrate, show or prove.
parole.testo: From Middle English demonstratif, from Middle French démonstratif, from Latin dēmōnstrātīvus. Equivalent to demonstrate + -ive.

parole.significato: To demonstrate.
parole.testo: From Middle French demonstrer, from Old French demonstrer, demoustrer, from Latin dēmonstrō, with re-Latinized spelling.

parole.significato: To indicate; to mark.
parole.testo: From Middle French denoter, from Latin denotare, from de- (“complete”) and notare (“to mark out”).

parole.significato: Having relatively high density.
parole.testo: From Middle French dense, from Latin dēnsus, from Proto-Indo-European *dens- (“thick, dense”) (whence also Ancient Greek δασύς (dasús)).

parole.significato: The amount of a certain phenomenon (such as stuff, things, energy, or otherwise) in a given area (surface area) or volu…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French densité or Latin densitas. Morphologically dense + -ity.

parole.significato: Relating to, or bearing, teeth.
parole.testo: From Middle French dentaire.

parole.significato: The act of stripping off covering, or removing the surface; a making bare.
parole.testo: From Middle French dénudation, from Latin denudatio.

parole.significato: To divest of all covering; to make bare or naked; to strip.
parole.testo: From Middle French dénuder, from Latin dēnūdāre, from dē- + nūdus (“bare”).

parole.significato: A part, portion, or subdivision.
parole.testo: From Middle English departement (“ceasing, end”), from Middle French département. Later senses borrowed from Modern French département. Doublet of département.

parole.significato: The state of being dependent, of relying upon another.
parole.testo: From Middle French dépendance. Morphologically depend + -ence.

parole.significato: Relying upon; depending upon.
parole.testo: From Middle English dependaunt, dependent, from Middle French dependant (present participle of dependre (“to depend”)) and Latin dēpendēns (present participle of dēpendeō (“to depend”)). By surface analysis, depend + -ent.

parole.significato: Synonym of loss or destruction.
parole.testo: From Middle French deperdition (French déperdition).

parole.significato: To bewail; to weep bitterly over; to feel sorrow for.
parole.testo: From Middle French déplorer, from Old French deplorer, from Latin dēplōrāre (“to lament over, bewail”), from dē- + plōrāre (“to wail, weep aloud”); origin uncertain.

parole.significato: The act of deporting or exiling, or the state of being deported; banishment; transportation.
parole.testo: From Middle French déportation, equivalent to deport + -ation.

parole.significato: Bearing; manner of presenting oneself.
parole.testo: From Late Middle French deportement (French déportement). By surface analysis, deport + -ment.

parole.significato: Detraction; depreciation.
parole.testo: From Middle French dépravation, from Latin dēprāvātiō (“perversion, distortion, corruption, depravity”).

parole.significato: The act of deprecating.
parole.testo: From Middle French deprecation (French: déprécation), from Latin dēprecātiōnem, from dēprecātiō (“deprecation, invocation”), from dēprecor (“to avert, warn off; to deprecate”).

parole.significato: Tending to deprecate.
parole.testo: From Middle French déprécatif.

parole.significato: An act of consuming agricultural resources (crops, livestock), especially as plunder.
parole.testo: From Middle French déprédation, from Latin depraedatio.

parole.significato: The act of deputing, or of appointing or commissioning a deputy or representative; office of a deputy or delegate; vice…
parole.testo: From Middle French députation, from Late Latin deputatio.

parole.significato: Laughable, ridiculous, especially due to being small, inadequate, or low-quality; provoking derision.
parole.testo: From Middle French dérisoire.

parole.significato: A leading or drawing off of water from a stream or source.
parole.testo: From Middle English derivacioun, borrowed from Middle French dérivation, from Latin dērīvātiō, dērīvātiōnem. Morphologically derive + -ation.

parole.significato: Obtained by derivation; not radical, original, or fundamental.
parole.testo: From Middle French dérivatif, from Latin dērīvātus, perfect passive participle of dērīvō (“to derive”). Related to derive; by surface analysis, derive + -ative.

parole.significato: Descending; going down.
parole.testo: From Middle English dessendaunte, borrowed from Middle French, from Latin dēscendēns, present participle of descendere, from dē + scandere (“to climb, ascend”).

parole.significato: The act of deserting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French désertion.

parole.significato: The state or process of being desiccated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dessiccation, from Late Latin desiccatio, desiccationem, from Latin desicco.

parole.significato: To cease to proceed or act; to stop (often with from).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French desister, from Latin dēsistō, from dē- + sistō (whence de-).

parole.significato: The act of desolating or laying waste; destruction of inhabitants; depopulation.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English desolacioun, from Middle French, Old French desolacion f, from Latin dēsōlātiō f.

parole.significato: A ruler with absolute power; a tyrant.
parole.testo: From Middle French despote, from Old French despote, from Medieval Latin despota, from Ancient Greek δεσπότης (despótēs, “lord, master, owner”). Cognate with Sanskrit दम्पति (dámpati).

parole.significato: The last course of a meal, consisting of fruit, sweet confections etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dessert, from desservir (“disserve”), from dés- (“dis-”) and servir (“serve”), thus literally meaning “removal of what has been served”. Note: It was erroneously suggested (e.g. in "Glucose syrups: Technology and Applications" (Peter Hull, 2010)) that the word is derived

parole.significato: Causing destruction; damaging.
parole.testo: From Middle English destructyve, from Middle French destructif, from Latin dēstrūctīvus, from past participle of dēstruere (“to tear down, destroy”) + -īvus.

parole.significato: The state when something (for example, a custom or a law) is no longer observed nor practised; disuse, obsolescence.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English desuetude, dissuetude (“discontinuance of a practice, disuse”), from Middle French désuétude (“obsolescence”) (modern French désuétude), from Latin dēsuētūdo (“discontinuance of a practice or a habit, disuse”), from dēsuētus + -tūdō (“suffix forming abstract nouns indicating

parole.significato: A part small enough to escape casual notice.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French détail, from Old French detail, from detaillier, from de- + taillier (“to cut”). Compare typologically Bulgarian подробност (podrobnost), Czech podrobnost, Russian подро́бность (podróbnostʹ) (akin to дроби́ть (drobítʹ)).

parole.significato: The act of detaining or the state of being detained; hindrance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French détention, from Latin detentio, detentionem. Equivalent to detain + -tion.

parole.significato: An ideogram used to mark semantic categories of words in logographic scripts.
parole.testo: From Middle French déterminatif. Equivalent to determine + -ative.

parole.significato: To dislike (someone or something) intensely; to loathe.
parole.testo: PIE word  *tréyes From Middle French detester (French détester), from Latin dētestor (“to imprecate evil while calling the gods to witness", "denounce", "hate intensely”), from dē- + testor (“to testify, bear witness”), from testis (“a witness”); see test, testify. Doublet of detestate.

parole.significato: Stimulating disgust or detestation; offensive; shocking.
parole.testo: From Middle French détestable. By surface analysis, detest + -able.

parole.significato: Hate coupled with disgust; abhorrence.
parole.testo: From Middle French détestation.

parole.significato: To take away; to withdraw or remove.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French détracter, from Latin detractum, past participle of detraho.

parole.significato: The act of devastating, or the state of being devastated; a laying waste.
parole.testo: From Middle French dévastation.

parole.significato: To divest; to undress.
parole.testo: From Middle French devester (“strip of possessions”), from Old French desvestir, from des- (“dis-”) + vestir (“to clothe”).

parole.significato: The act of deviating; wandering off the correct or true path or road.
parole.testo: From Middle French deviation, from Medieval Latin deviatio. Morphologically deviate + -ion.

parole.significato: The act of leaving real property in a will.
parole.testo: From Middle French devise. Doublet of device.

parole.significato: Duty, business; something that one must do.
parole.testo: From Middle English devoir, borrowed from Middle French devoir, from Old French deveir, from Latin dēbēre (“to owe; ought, must”).

parole.significato: A rolling down.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dévolution, from Medieval Latin devolutio, devolutionis, from Latin devolvo.

parole.significato: Skill in performing tasks, especially with the hands.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dextérité, from Latin dexteritas, from dexter (“on the right”), this is in reference to most people having greater fine motor skills in their right hand. Partially displaced native Old English handcræft, whence Modern English handcraft.

parole.significato: Of, being, or pertaining to a devil or the Devil.
parole.testo: From Middle English diabolik, from Middle French diabolique, from Late Latin diabolicus, from Ancient Greek διαβολικός (diabolikós, “devilish”), from διάβολος (diábolos, “devil”). First attested in 1350–1400.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a deacon or the diaconate.
parole.testo: From Middle French diaconal, from Latin diaconus (“deacon”).

parole.significato: Joining two nonadjacent vertices (of a polygon or polyhedron).
parole.testo: From Middle French diagonal, from Latin diagōnālis, from Ancient Greek διαγώνιος (diagṓnios, “from angle to angle”), from διά (diá, “across”) + γωνία (gōnía, “angle”).

parole.significato: A graduated, circular scale over which a needle moves to show a measurement (such as speed).
parole.testo: The original meaning was 'sundial' and/or 'clock dial'; from Middle English diall, from Middle French dyal, from Latin diālis (“daily, concerning the day”), because of its use in telling the time of day, from Latin diēs (“day”). Compare Spanish dial and día (“day”).

parole.significato: A lect (often a regional or minority language) as part of a group or family of languages, especially if they are viewed…
parole.testo: From Middle French dialecte, from Latin dialectos, dialectus, from Ancient Greek διάλεκτος (diálektos, “conversation, the language of a country or a place or a nation, the local idiom which derives from a dominant language”), from διαλέγομαι (dialégomai, “to participate in a dialogue”), from διά (di

parole.significato: Consisting of or resembling diamond.
parole.testo: From Middle French diamantin, from diamant (“diamond”) + -in (“-ine”).

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or measured across a diameter.
parole.testo: From Middle French dyametral, from Medieval Latin diametrālis.

parole.significato: Something transparent.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French diaphane, from Medieval Latin diaphanus (“transparent”), borrowed from Ancient Greek δῐᾰφᾰνής (dĭăphănḗs), from δῐᾰφαίνω (dĭăphaínō, “to shine; to be manifest”) + -ής (-ḗs, adjectival suffix). By surface analysis, dia- + -phane.

parole.significato: A gastrointestinal disorder characterized by frequent and very soft or watery bowel movements.
parole.testo: From Middle English diaria, from Middle French diarrie (French diarrhée), from Late Latin diarrhoea, from Ancient Greek διάρροια (diárrhoia, “through-flowing”), from διά (diá, “through”) + ῥέω (rhéō, “flow”). By surface analysis, dia- + -rrhea. Spelling later altered to resemble the word's Latin and

parole.significato: Dated spelling of diarrhoea.
parole.testo: From Middle French diarrie (French diarrhée), from Late Latin diarrhoea, from Ancient Greek διάρροια (diárrhoia, “through-flowing”), from διά (diá, “through”) + ῥέω (rhéō, “flow”). Spelling later altered to resemble the word's Latin and Greek roots.

parole.significato: Synonym of dictate.
parole.testo: From Middle French dictatorie, from Classical Latin dictātor + Middle French -ie. By surface analysis, dictate + -ory.

parole.significato: Office of a dictator; dictatorship.
parole.testo: From Middle English dictature, from Middle French dictature and its etymon Classical Latin dictātūra. By surface analysis, dictate + -ure.

parole.significato: The state of being difficult, or hard to do.
parole.testo: From Middle English difficulte, from Middle French and Anglo-Norman difficulte and their etymon Latin difficultas, from difficul, older form of difficilis (“hard to do, difficult”), from dis- + facilis (“easy”); see difficile and difficult. Equivalent to dis- + facile + -ty. Also analysable as diffi

parole.significato: irregularity or diversity of form; lack of uniformity
parole.testo: From Middle French difformité. See difform, deformity.

parole.significato: To spread (something) over or through as in air, water, or other matter, especially by fluid motion or passive means.
parole.testo: From Middle French diffuser, from Latin diffūsus, past participle of diffundere, from dis- + fundere.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a diocese.
parole.testo: From Middle French diocesain.

parole.significato: That which directs; serving to direct, indicate, or guide.
parole.testo: From Middle French directif. The noun senses are from French directive (feminine form of the adjective).

parole.significato: One who directs; the person in charge of managing a department or directorate (e.g., director of engineering), project,…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French directeur and its source Late Latin dīrēctōrem, from Latin dīrēctus. By surface analysis, direct + -or.

parole.significato: Causing repugnance; unpleasant to the feelings or senses; displeasing.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English disagreable, from Middle French desagreable, from Old French desagraable (compare French désagréable). By surface analysis, dis- + agreeable.

parole.significato: To sadden or displease (someone) by underperforming, or by not delivering something promised or hoped for.
parole.testo: From Middle French desapointer (compare French désappointer). The word originally meant to "dispossess of appointed office", and eventually broadened to mean "to frustrate the expectations or desires of" and "defeat the realization or fulfillment of".

parole.significato: To throw into disorder; to break the array of.
parole.testo: From Middle English disareyen (“to disarray”), from Middle French desarroyer, from Old French desareer, from des- (“dis-”) + areer (“to array”).

parole.significato: An unexpected natural or man-made catastrophe of substantial extent causing significant physical damage or destruction,…
parole.testo: From Middle French desastre, from Italian disastro, from dis- + astro (“star”), from Latin astrum (“star”), from Ancient Greek ἄστρον (ástron, “star”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr.

parole.significato: Of the nature of a disaster; calamitous.
parole.testo: From disaster + -ous, after Middle French desastreux (modern French désastreux; from desastre (modern French désastre, “disaster”; from des- + astre, a calque of Italian disastro) + -eux), itself after Italian disastroso, from disastro + -oso, from dis- (“away, without”) (from Latin dis-) + astro (“

parole.significato: To break up or (cause to) cease to exist; to disperse.
parole.testo: Attested since the 1590s, from Middle French desbander (Modern French débander), from des- (English dis-) + bande (English band), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ- (“to tie”). By surface analysis, dis- + band.

parole.significato: To disembark.
parole.testo: From Middle French desbarquer, from des- + barque.

parole.significato: Possible to discern; detectable or derivable by use of the senses or the intellect.
parole.testo: From Middle French discernable; spelling changed from -a- to -i- in the 17th century to conform to Latin discernibilis. By surface analysis, discern + -ible.

parole.significato: The act of distinguishing between things.
parole.testo: From Middle French discernement, equivalent to discern + -ment.

parole.significato: To open up; unfasten.
parole.testo: From Middle English disclosen, from Middle French desclos, from Old French desclore, itself from Vulgar Latin disclaudere, from Latin dis- + claudere (“to close, shut”) or as a variant of discludo, discludere (cf. disclude). By surface analysis, dis- + close.

parole.significato: To upset the composure of; to startle.
parole.testo: From Middle French desconcerter, from des- (“dis-”) + concerter (“to bring into agreement, organize”).

parole.significato: A state of being discordant; disagreement, inconsistency.
parole.testo: From Middle French discordance. By surface analysis, discord + -ance.

parole.significato: To have an unfavorable opinion of; to deprecate or disapprove of.
parole.testo: From Middle French descontenancer (compare French décontenancer).

parole.significato: To extinguish the courage of; to dishearten; to depress the spirits of; to deprive of confidence; to deject.
parole.testo: From Middle French descourager (modern French décourager), from Old French descouragier, from des- and corage. By surface analysis, dis- + courage.

parole.significato: Verbal exchange, conversation.
parole.testo: From Middle English discours, borrowed from Middle French discours (“conversation, speech”), from Latin discursus (“the act of running about”), from Latin discurrō (“run about”), from dis- (“apart”) + currō (“run”). Spelling modified by influence of Middle French cours (“course”). Doublet of discurs

parole.significato: One who discovers: a person who has discovered something.
parole.testo: From Middle English discoverour, dyscowerer, partly from Middle French descouvreur and partly equivalent to discover + -er.

parole.significato: Of or concerning discourse.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French discursif, formed from the stem of Latin discursus and the suffix -if, and in part borrowed from Medieval Latin discursivus. By surface analysis, discourse + -ive.

parole.significato: To converse or debate concerning a particular topic.
parole.testo: From Middle English discussen, from Middle French and Anglo-Norman discusser (French discuter), from Latin discussus, past participle of discutiō (“to strike or shake apart, break up, scatter; examine, discuss”), from dis- (“apart”) + quatiō (“to shake”).

parole.significato: To free from illusion, false belief or enchantment; to undeceive or disillusion.
parole.testo: From Middle French desenchanter, equivalent to dis- + enchant.

parole.significato: A circular movement of the blade that avoids the opponent's parry
parole.testo: From Middle French désengager ; dis- + engage.

parole.significato: Lack of favour; displeasure.
parole.testo: From English dis- + favour, from Middle French desfaveur.

parole.significato: To vomit or spew, to discharge.
parole.testo: From Middle French desgorger.

parole.significato: The condition of being out of favor; loss of favor, regard, or respect.
parole.testo: From Middle French disgracier.

parole.significato: To cause an intense dislike for something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French desgouster, from Old French desgouster (“to put off one's appetite”), from des- (“dis-”) + gouster, goster (“to taste”), from Latin gustus (“a tasting”). By surface analysis, dis- + gust (“taste”). The noun is from Middle French desgoust, from the verb.

parole.significato: To sterilize by the use of cleaning agent.
parole.testo: From English dis- + infect, from Middle French desinfecter.

parole.significato: Not connected; separated.
parole.testo: From Middle English disjunctief, disjunctyf, from Middle French disjunctif and Latin disjunctīvus (“placed in opposition”).

parole.significato: To take apart; to disassemble; to take to pieces.
parole.testo: From Middle French desmanteler, itself from des- (“dis-”), mantel (“coat”) + -er (verbal suffix). By surface analysis, dis- + mantle. Compare typologically uncloak, reveal, unmask.

parole.significato: A dime minted in 1792.
parole.testo: From Middle French dixme, Old French disme (“tenth, tithe”), from Latin decimus (“tenth”). Doublet of dime.

parole.significato: to be unwilling to oblige; to disappoint, to inconvenience, not to cooperate.
parole.testo: From Middle French desobliger. By surface analysis, dis- + oblige.

parole.significato: Absence of order; state of not being arranged in an orderly manner.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French desordre (modern French désordre), from Old French desordre, from des- + ordre; by surface analysis, dis- + order (<< Latin ōrdō). Compare typologically Russian непоря́док (neporjádok), беспоря́док (besporjádok), неуря́дица (neurjádica) (akin to ряд (rjad), поря́док (porj

parole.significato: The state of being unequal; difference.
parole.testo: From Middle French disparité, from Latin disparitātem, accusative of disparitās, from dispār + -tās, from dis- + pār. By surface analysis, dis- + parity.

parole.significato: To scatter in different directions.
parole.testo: From Middle French disperser, from Latin dispersus, past participle of dispergō (“to scatter abroad, disperse”), from dis- (“apart”) + spargō (“to scatter”); see sparse.

parole.significato: To put out of place; to disarrange.
parole.testo: From Middle French desplacer (French: déplacer).

parole.significato: The way in which something or someone is disposed or disposed of (in any sense of those terms); thus:
parole.testo: From Middle English disposicioun, from Middle French disposition, from Latin dispositiōnem, accusative singular of dispositiō, from dispōnō. By surface analysis, dispose + -ition. Doublet of dispositio.

parole.significato: Intending to, resulting in, or capable of disposition (disposing, disposing of, or settling a matter).
parole.testo: From Middle French dispositif and its source, Latin dispositus. Compare Piedmontese dispositiv.

parole.significato: To deprive someone of the possession of land, especially by evicting them.
parole.testo: From Middle English [Term?], from Middle French despossesser. Equivalent to dis- + possess.

parole.significato: An act of expressing dissent, especially spoken.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English dissencioun, from Middle French dissention, discention, from Old French dissension, from Latin dissensio.

parole.significato: A harsh, discordant combination of sounds.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dissonance, from Latin dissonantia; by surface analysis, dis- + son- + -ance.

parole.significato: Exhibiting dissonance; not agreeing; not harmonizing or melodizing.
parole.testo: From Middle French dissonant.

parole.significato: To convince not to try or do.
parole.testo: From Middle French dissuader, from Latin dissuādeō (“to urge differently”, “to advise against”, “to dissuade”), from dis- (“away from”, “asunder”) + suādeō (“to recommend”, “to advise”, “to urge”).

parole.significato: the act or an instance of dissuading
parole.testo: From Middle English dissuasioun, from Middle French dissuasion.

parole.significato: Tending to dissuade, or divert from a measure or purpose; dehortatory.
parole.testo: From Middle French dissuasif.

parole.significato: The act of distending.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French; cf. Latin distentio.

parole.significato: Something that distracts.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French distraction, from Latin distractio. Equivalent to distract + -ion.

parole.significato: Relating to distribution.
parole.testo: From Middle French distributif, from Latin distribūtīvus.

parole.significato: Separation (disintegration) of a union; lack of union where union would be desirable.
parole.testo: From Middle French désunion.

parole.significato: Synonym of diversify.
parole.testo: Hypercorrection of diversify, on the basis of Latin dīversificō + -ate (verb-forming suffix) with diversify being the regular derived form of Middle French diversifier, itself from Medieval Latin dīversificō, from Latin dīversus (“opposite, different”).

parole.significato: To make (something) diverse or varied in form or quality; to give variety to (something) to distinguish by numerous asp…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French diversifier, equivalent to diverse + -ify.

parole.significato: To strip, deprive, or dispossess (someone) of something (such as a right, passion, privilege, or prejudice).
parole.testo: Alteration of devest, from Middle French devester (“strip of possessions”), from Old French desvestir, from des- (“dis-”) + vestir (“to clothe”).

parole.significato: A cash payment of money by a company to its shareholders, usually made periodically (e.g., quarterly or annually).
parole.testo: From Middle French dividende, from Latin dīvidendum (“thing to be divided”), future passive participle of dīvidō (“to divide”), by surface analysis, divide + -end.

parole.significato: To foretell (something), especially by the use of divination.
parole.testo: Replaced Middle English devine, devin from Middle French deviner, from Latin dīvīnō.

parole.significato: Ready to accept instruction or direction; obedient; subservient.
parole.testo: From Middle English docyle, from Middle French docile, from Latin docilis, from docēre (“teach”). Compare Portuguese dócil ("docile").

parole.significato: The quality of being docile.
parole.testo: From Middle French docilité, from Latin docilitas.

parole.significato: An original or official paper used as the basis, proof, or support of anything else, including any writing, book, or ot…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French document, from Latin documentum.

parole.significato: Adhering only to principles which are true a priori, rather than truths based on evidence or deduction.
parole.testo: From Middle French dogmatique and its etymon, Late Latin dogmaticus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek δογματικός (dogmatikós, “didactic”), from δόγμα (dógma, “dogma”).

parole.significato: A structural element resembling the hollow upper half of a sphere.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dome, domme (modern French dôme), from Italian duomo, from Latin domus (ecclesiae) (literally “house (of the church)”), a calque of Ancient Greek οἶκος τῆς ἐκκλησίας (oîkos tês ekklēsías). Doublet of domus and duomo.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the home.
parole.testo: From Middle French domestique, from Latin domesticus, from domus (“house, home”).

parole.significato: A home or residence.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English domicelle, domicylie, from Middle French domicile and directly from Latin domicilium.

parole.significato: The division of the heavens into twelve astrological houses; or a particular system for such division.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French domification; equivalent to domify + -ification.

parole.significato: To divide (the heavens) into different astrological houses.
parole.testo: From Middle French domifier.

parole.significato: The fifth major tone of a musical scale (five major steps above the note in question); thus G is the dominant of C, A o…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dominant.

parole.significato: Power or the use of power; sovereignty over something; stewardship, supremacy.
parole.testo: From Middle English dominion, from Middle French dominion, from Latin dominium (“lordship, right of ownership”), from dominus (“lord”), from domus (“house”). See demain, demesne, domain, dominium.

parole.significato: A voluntary gift or contribution for a specific cause.
parole.testo: From Middle English donacion, donation, from Middle French donation, from Latin dōnātiō (“a present”), from dōnō (“to give”), from dōnum (“a gift”). Recorded in English since the 15th century. Equivalent to donate + -ion.

parole.significato: The process of falling asleep.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dormition, from Latin dormītiōnem.

parole.significato: A dreamlike semi-conscious state, such as while falling asleep or waking up, between periods of sleep, or from exhausti…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dorveille.

parole.significato: A measured portion of medicine taken at any one time.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dose, from Late Latin dosis, from Ancient Greek δόσις (dósis, “a portion prescribed”, literally “a giving”), used by Galen and other Greek physicians to mean an amount of medicine, from δίδωμι (dídōmi, “to give”). Mostly displaced English drench. Doublet of doos.

parole.significato: Dowry.
parole.testo: From Middle English dote (“endowment”) (c. 1450), from Middle French dote (modern dot), from Latin dos.

parole.significato: To endow, donate.
parole.testo: From Middle French doter, Latin dōtāre.

parole.significato: Capable of being endowed.
parole.testo: From Middle French dowable; equivalent to dow + -able.

parole.significato: A widow holding property or title derived from her late husband.
parole.testo: From Middle French douagere, douagiere, from douage (“dower”), from the verb douer (“to endow”), from Latin dōtō (“to endow”), from dōs (“dowry”).

parole.significato: A small dragon.
parole.testo: From Middle English dragonet, from Middle French dragonet. By surface analysis, dragon + -et.

parole.significato: A West Indian coasting vessel, with long masts and lateen sails.
parole.testo: From Middle French drogueur (“ship for catching and drying fish”), from Dutch drogher, droogher, from droogen (“to dry”).

parole.significato: To administer intoxicating drugs to, generally without the recipient's knowledge or consent.
parole.testo: From Middle English drogge (“medicine”), from Middle French drogue, drocque (“tincture, pharmaceutical product”) (c. 1462), from Middle Dutch or Middle Low German droge, as in droge vate (“dry vats, dry barrels”), mistaking droge for the contents, which were usually dried herbs, plants or wares. Dro

parole.significato: The process of doubting or the state of being in doubt; hesitation, uncertainty.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English dubytacion, from Middle French dubitation, from Latin dubitātiō.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a duke, a duchess, or the duchy or dukedom they hold.
parole.testo: From Middle French ducal, from Latin ducālis. Doublet of dogal.

parole.significato: A gold coin minted by various European nations.
parole.testo: From Middle French ducat, late Old French ducat, from Old Italian ducato, from Medieval Latin ducātus, from oblique stem of dux (“duke; leader”). Doublet of duchy.

parole.significato: The act of duplicating.
parole.testo: From Middle English duplicacioun, from Middle French duplication, from Late Latin duplicātiō, duplicātiōnem, from Latin duplicō. Morphologically duplicate + -ion.

parole.significato: A series of rulers or dynasts from one family.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dynastie, from Late Latin dynastia, from Ancient Greek δυναστεία (dunasteía, “power, dominion”).

parole.significato: Not at or in the centre; away from the centre.
parole.testo: From Middle French excentrique, from Medieval Latin eccentricus, from Ancient Greek ἔκκεντρος (ékkentros, “not having the earth as the center of an orbit”), from ἐκ (ek, “out”) + κέντρον (kéntron, “point”). Equivalent to ex- + -centric.

parole.significato: Now chiefly home economics: the art or science of household management, especially relating to the appropriate organiza…
parole.testo: From economic (noun) (obsolete) + -s (suffix forming pluralia tantum, and regular plural forms of nouns). Economic is derived from Middle English economike, iconomique (“household management”), and then: * from Middle French iconomique, oeconomique, and Old French iconomike (“(noun) household manage

parole.significato: An expert in economics, especially one who studies economic data and extracts higher-level information or proposes theo…
parole.testo: From Middle French économiste (“household manager”). By surface analysis, economy + -ist.

parole.significato: To erase (as anything impressed or inscribed upon a surface); to render illegible or indiscernible.
parole.testo: From Middle French effacer (“erase”), from Old French esfacier (“remove the face”).

parole.significato: Efficacy.
parole.testo: From Middle French efficacité (whence -acity).

parole.significato: To force oneself.
parole.testo: From Middle French efforcer.

parole.significato: The work involved in performing an activity; exertion.
parole.testo: From Middle French effort, from Old French esfort, deverbal of esforcier (“to force, exert”), from Vulgar Latin *exfortiō, from Latin ex + fortis (“strong”). Compare typologically Bulgarian усилие (usilie), Czech úsilí, Polish wysiłek, Russian уси́лие (usílije) (< Proto-Slavic *sila).

parole.significato: To frighten, startle.
parole.testo: From Middle French effrayer.

parole.significato: To give self-confidence to.
parole.testo: From Middle French effronter, from Old French esfronter, from Late Latin effrontō, from the prefix ex- (“from”) + frōns (“forehead”).

parole.significato: Poured out freely; profuse.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French effuser, from Latin effusus, past participle of effundere (“to pour out”).

parole.significato: A liquid outpouring.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French effusion, from Latin effūsiō (“outpouring”). Displaced native Old English āgotennes.

parole.significato: Equality.
parole.testo: From Middle English egalitee, from Middle French egalité, esgalité.

parole.significato: The act of ejecting.
parole.testo: From Middle French éjection, from Latin eiectio.

parole.significato: The act or process of producing or refining with labor; improvement by successive operations; refinement.
parole.testo: From Middle French élaboration. Morphologically elaborate + -ion.

parole.significato: To pass or move by.
parole.testo: From Middle French elapser, from Latin elapsus.

parole.significato: Grace, refinement, and beauty in movement, appearance, or manners.
parole.testo: From Middle French élégance, from Latin ēlegantia (“exquisiteness; refinement, elegance”).

parole.significato: Characterised by or exhibiting elegance; having grace, refinement, or tasteful simplicity.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English elegaunt, from Middle French elegant, ultimately from Latin ēlegāns, collateral form of present participle of ēligere, from ex- (“out of, from”) + legō (“choose, select, appoint”).

parole.significato: Of or relating to an elegy.
parole.testo: From Middle French élégiaque, from Latin elegīacus, from Ancient Greek ἐλεγειακός (elegeiakós).

parole.significato: A mournful or plaintive poem; a funeral song; a poem of lamentation.
parole.testo: From Middle French elegie, from Latin elegīa, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐλεγείᾱ (elegeíā), ellipsis of ἐλεγείᾱ ᾠδή (elegeíā ōidḗ, “an elegiac song”).

parole.significato: Allowed to and meeting the necessary conditions required to participate in or be chosen for something.
parole.testo: From Middle French eligible, from Latin eligibilis, from ēligō (“to select, to choose”).

parole.significato: Enamel (“an opaque, glossy coating”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French email, from Old French esmal (“enamel”) (modern French émail (“enamel; vitreous enamel; glaze (coating on pottery)”)), from Medieval Latin smaltum (“enamel”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meld- (“to melt; to soften”). Doublet of smalt, smalto, and schmaltz.

parole.significato: To treat a corpse with preservatives in order to prevent decomposition.
parole.testo: From Middle English enbawmen, from Middle French embaumer, from Old French embasmer. See balm.

parole.significato: To enclose (as though behind bars); to imprison.
parole.testo: From Middle French embarrer, from barre (“bar”).

parole.significato: To go aboard a craft or vessel for transportation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French embarquer, from em- + barque (“small ship”). Compare with Portuguese embarcar, Spanish abarcar.

parole.significato: The function or duty of an ambassador.
parole.testo: Modern variant of obsolete ambassy, from Middle French ambassee (“mission, embassy”), from Old French ambascee (also enbassee (“message for a high official, official mission”)) from Old Italian ambasciata, from Old Occitan ambaissada (“embassy”), derived from ambaissa (“message”), from Late Latin am

parole.significato: The art of decorating fabric or other materials using a needle to stitch thread or yarn.
parole.testo: From Middle French embrouderie, from embrouder + -erie. By surface analysis, embroider + -y.

parole.significato: To come into view.
parole.testo: First attested in the late 16th century. Borrowed from Middle French emerger, from Latin ēmergō (“to rise up or out”), from ē- (a variant of ex- (“out, forth”)) + mergō (“to dip, to sink”)

parole.significato: Noteworthy, remarkable, great.
parole.testo: From Middle French éminent, from Latin present participle ēminēns, ēminentis, from verb ēmineō (“to project, protrude”), from ex- (“out of, from”) + mineō, related to mons (English mount). Compare with imminent. Unrelated to emanate, which is instead from mānō (“to flow”). Displaced native Old Engli

parole.significato: A prince, commander or other leader or ruler in an Islamic nation.
parole.testo: From Middle French emir, from Ottoman Turkish امیر (emir), from Arabic أَمِير (ʔamīr, “commander, prince”). Doublet of amir, Amir, admiral, and amira.

parole.significato: Something which is emitted or sent out; issue.
parole.testo: First attested in 1607. From Middle French émission, from Latin ēmissiō (“sending forth”), from ēmittō (“send out”), from ex (“from, out of”) + mittō (“send”).

parole.significato: Movement; agitation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French emotion (modern French émotion), from émouvoir (“excite”), based on Latin ēmōtus, past participle of ēmoveō (“to move out, move away, remove, stir up, irritate”), from ē- (“out”) (variant of ex-), and moveō (“move”).

parole.significato: The occupation or work for which one is used, and often paid.
parole.testo: From employ (itself from Middle French employer, from Middle French empleier, from Latin implicō (“enfold, involve, be connected with”), itself from in- + plicō (“fold”)) + -ment.

parole.significato: The endeavor or desire to equal or excel someone else in qualities or actions.
parole.testo: From Middle French émulation, from Latin aemulātiō.

parole.significato: To set (a gemstone, etc.) into.
parole.testo: From Middle English enchacen, enchasen, from Middle French enchasser.

parole.significato: The act of encouraging
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French encoragement.
