parole.significato: Belonging to or characteristic of the sea; existing or found in the sea; formed or produced by the sea.
parole.testo: Recorded since c.1420 as Middle English marin, borrowed from Middle French marin, from Old French, from Latin marinus (“of the sea”), itself from mare (“sea”), from Proto-Indo-European *móri (“body of water, lake”) (cognate with Old English mere (“sea, lake, pool, pond”), Dutch meer, German Meer, al

parole.significato: Pertaining to marriage.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French marital, and its source, Latin marītālis, from marītus (“husband”).

parole.significato: Relating to or connected with the sea or its uses (as navigation, commerce, etc.).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French maritime, from Latin maritimus.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French marmouset (“a gargoyle; a small child”), probably from marmouser (“to mumble”), of imitative origin.

parole.significato: Any of several large ground-dwelling rodents of the genera Marmota and Cynomys in the squirrel family.

parole.significato: A decorative technique in which veneers of wood, ivory, metal etc. are inlaid into a wooden surface to form intricate d…
parole.testo: From Middle French marqueterie.

parole.significato: The territory held by a marquis, margrave or marchioness.
parole.testo: From marquis + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office, the concrete charge of it), on the pattern of Middle French marquisat, Italian marchesato.

parole.significato: The Turk's cap lily (Lilium martagon).
parole.testo: From Middle French martagon, from Old Anatolian Turkish [Term?] (Ottoman Turkish مارطغان, modern Turkish martağan), originally a style of turban.

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or suggestive of war; warlike.
parole.testo: From Middle English martial, marcial, mercial, mercialle (“relating to war, warlike; military; for use in fighting or warfare; brave, hardy; combative, fierce; ruthless, vicious; domineering, overbearing”), from Middle French martial (modern French martial (“martial”)), or directly from its etymon L

parole.testo: From Middle French martin (French martinet).

parole.testo: From Middle French martingale, from Occitan martegalo, feminine form of martegal, an inhabitant of Martigues, which is from Latin maritima. Possibly merged with Spanish almártaga. parole.significato: A bird, the martin.
parole.testo: From Middle English martilet, probably a blend of martinet (“martin”; from Middle French martinet and Medieval Latin martineta) and Middle French merlet.

parole.significato: A cover, or partial cover, for the face, used for disguise or protection.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French masque (“a covering to hide or protect the face”), from Italian maschera (“mask, disguise”), from (a byform of, see it for more) Medieval Latin masca, mascha, a borrowing of Proto-West Germanic *maskā, from which English mesh and mask (“mesh”) (below at Etymology 2) are i

parole.significato: Very large in size or extent.
parole.testo: From Middle English massif, from Middle French massif, equivalent to mass + -ive. The Irish sense is possibly derived from Irish mas (“fine, handsome”).

parole.significato: A sailor.
parole.testo: From Middle French matelot (“sailor”). Compare Dutch matroos and German Matrose. Doublet of matross.

parole.significato: An expert on mathematics; someone who studies mathematics.
parole.testo: From Middle English mathematicion, from Middle French mathematicien, from mathematique f sg (“mathematics”) (from Latin mathēmatica, feminine of mathēmaticus, from Ancient Greek μαθηματικός (mathēmatikós, “fond of learning”), from μάθημα (máthēma, “knowledge, learning”) + -ικός (-ikós)) + Middle Fre

parole.significato: morning
parole.testo: From Middle French matin, from Latin mātūtīnum (“the morning”).

parole.significato: Synonym of matutinal.
parole.testo: A variant of matutinal (possibly influenced by French matin (“morning”)), which is borrowed from Middle French matutinal (modern French matutinal), and from its etymon Late Latin mātūtīnālis (“(adjective) belonging to the morning; of or pertaining to matins; (noun) morning hymn or psalm; book of lau

parole.significato: Of, or having to do with matrimony and marriage.
parole.testo: From Middle French matrimonial, also matrimony + -al.

parole.significato: The process of becoming mature.
parole.testo: From Middle English maturacioun, from Middle French maturation, from Latin maturatio. By surface analysis, mature + -ation.

parole.significato: A remedy used in medieval medicine to promote maturation; a maturant.
parole.testo: From Middle English maturatif, from Middle French maturatif, from Medieval Latin mātūrātīvus. By surface analysis, mature + -ative or maturate + -ive.

parole.significato: Fully developed; grown up in terms of physical appearance, behaviour or thinking; ripe.
parole.testo: From late Middle English mature, from Middle French mature, from Latin mātūrus. Doublet of maduro. Partially displaced ripe, from Old English rīpe (“ripe, mature”).

parole.significato: To proceed toward maturity: full development or completion (either of concrete or of abstract things, e.g. plans, judgm…
parole.testo: From Middle English maturen, from Middle French maturer (“to mature”), from Latin mātūrō.

parole.significato: Of, occurring in, or relating to the morning, especially the early morning upon waking up.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French matutinal (modern French matutinal), and from its etymon Late Latin mātūtīnālis (“(adjective) belonging to the morning; of or pertaining to matins; (noun) morning hymn or psalm; book of lauds”), from Latin mātūtīnus (“of, occurring in, or pertaining to the early morning,

parole.significato: The office of a mayor, or the tenure during which a particular mayor holds office, where the time span may encompass on…
parole.testo: From Middle English mairaltee, from Middle French mairalté.

parole.significato: An edible fish, of species Argyrosomus regius, of the family Sciaenidae, found from the Black Sea to the eastern Atlant…
parole.testo: From Middle French maigre.

parole.significato: A stamped metal disc used as a personal ornament, a charm, or a religious object.
parole.testo: From Middle English [Term?], from Middle French medaille, medale, from Italian medaglia (originally "half a denarius"), from Early Medieval Latin medālia, feminine derived via dissimilation (/dj–lj/ > /d–lj/) from mediālia, neuter plural of Late Latin mediālis (“middle”, adjective), from Classical L

parole.significato: A central vein or nerve, especially the median vein or median nerve running through the forearm and arm.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French median, from Latin mediānus (“of or pertaining to the middle”, adjective), from medius (“middle”) (see medium), from Proto-Indo-European *médʰyos (“middle”). Doublet of mean and mizzen. Cognate with Old English midde, middel (“middle”). More at middle.

parole.significato: Negotiation to resolve differences conducted by an impartial party.
parole.testo: From Middle English mediacion, mediacioun, medyacion, medyacyoun from Middle French mediacion and its etymon Late Latin mediātiō, from mediārī (“intervene”), from Latin medius (“middle”). By surface analysis, mediate + -ion.

parole.significato: One who negotiates between parties seeking mutual agreement.
parole.testo: From Middle English mediatour, mediatoure, mediatur, medyatour, from Middle French mediateur, mediatur or its etymon Latin mediātor (“one who mediates”), from mediātum, supine of mediō (“be in the middle”), from medius (“middle”). By surface analysis, mediate + -or.

parole.significato: A medicine, or all the medicines regularly taken by a patient.
parole.testo: From Middle English medicacioun, from Middle French médication and its etymon Latin medicātiō, from medicārī (“to heal, cure”), from medicus (“a physician, surgeon”), from medērī (“to heal”). Equivalent to medicate + -ion.

parole.significato: A substance which specifically promotes healing when ingested or consumed in some way; a pharmaceutical drug.
parole.testo: From Middle English medicin, from Middle French medicine, from Old French medecine, from Latin medicīna (“the healing art, medicine, a physician's shop, a remedy, medicine”), feminine of medicīnus (“of or belonging to physic or surgery, or to a physician or surgeon”), from medicus (“a physician, sur

parole.significato: The condition of being mediocre; having only an average degree of quality, skills etc.; no better than standard.
parole.testo: From Middle French médiocrité, from Latin mediocritās, from mediocris; by surface analysis, mediocre + -ity.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to meditation.
parole.testo: From Middle French méditatif.

parole.significato: A headache; a migraine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French migraigne, semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin hēmicrānia (“pain in one half of the head”), from Ancient Greek ἡμικρᾱνίᾰ (hēmikrāníă), from ἡμι- (hēmi-, “hemi-, half”) + κρανίον (kraníon, “skull”) (whence also English cranium). Doublet of migraine and hemicrania.

parole.significato: melancholy
parole.testo: From Middle English malencolious, from Middle French melancolieus.

parole.significato: Having a pleasant melody or sound; tuneful.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English melodious, from Middle French melodieus, melodieux. By surface analysis, melod(i) + -ous.

parole.significato: Having the qualities of, or pertaining to, a membrane.
parole.testo: From Middle French membraneux; equivalent to membrane + -ous.

parole.significato: Lying, untruthful or dishonest.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French mendacieux, from Latin mendācium (“lie, untruth”), from mendāx (“lying”), + -ious.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the mind or specifically the total emotional and intellectual response of an individual to external r…
parole.testo: Borrowing from Middle French mental, from Late Latin mentālis, from mēns (“mind, disposition; heart, soul”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: Relating to a meridian (in various senses); meridional.
parole.testo: PIE word  *médʰyos From Late Middle English meridian, meridien (“relating to midday or noon; southern; (astronomy) relating to the celestial meridian”) [and other forms], from Middle French meridien, Old French meridiane (“relating to midday; southern”) (whence Anglo-Norman meridien; modern French m

parole.significato: located in the south, southern; later especially, often pertaining to the southern parts of Europe.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French meridional, from Latin merīdiōnālis, from merīdiēs (“noon; south”).

parole.significato: To deserve, to earn.
parole.testo: From Middle English meriten, from Middle French meriter, Old French meriter (“to deserve, merit”) (modern French mériter), from merite: see further in Etymology 1. The word is cognate with Italian meritare (“to deserve, merit; to be worth; to earn”), Latin meritāre (“to earn regularly; to serve as a

parole.significato: Of or relating to the Merovings, the members of a Salian Frankish dynasty, descended from Merovech, that came to rule t…
parole.testo: From Middle French Merovingien (“of or relating to the Merovings, the descendants of Merovech”), from Medieval Latin Merovingī (“Merovings”) [plural of Merovingus, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *Mārīwīg (a male given name composed of *mārī (“famous”) + *wīg (“fight”)) + *-ing] + Middle French

parole.significato: A mixed race person, especially if mostly white in ancestry, appearance and culture.
parole.testo: Usually from Middle French mestis (“a person of mixed race”), from Latin mixtus (Modern French métis); cognate with Spanish mestizo. Doublet of Metis, metis, mestizo, and mustee. Sometimes from Colonial Louisiana French mestif "child of an Octoroon and a white person" (15/16 white, 1/16 black), from

parole.significato: Concealment, mystification, obfuscation.
parole.testo: Coined in translation of Rabelais' works, from Middle French matagrabolisme, from matagraboliser (“mystify”). The first element is from Ancient Greek μάταιος (mátaios, “vain, futile”), but altered to assimilate to the prefix meta-, + French grabeler (“sift, examine closely, scrutinize”) + -isme.

parole.significato: To puzzle, mystify.
parole.testo: From Middle French matagraboliser. See metagrobolism.

parole.significato: A substance of variable composition, but resembling a soft, dark-coloured metal, used in the bearings of machines to re…
parole.testo: From Middle English metallyne, from Middle French metalin and Latin metallinus. By surface analysis, metal + -ine.

parole.significato: The use of a word, phrase, concept, or set of concepts to refer to something other than its literal meaning, invoking a…
parole.testo: From Middle French métaphore, from Latin metaphora, from Ancient Greek μεταφορά (metaphorá), from μεταφέρω (metaphérō, “to transfer, apply”), from μετά (metá, “with, across, after”) + φέρω (phérō, “to bear, carry”).

parole.significato: An atmospheric or meteorological phenomenon. These were sometimes classified as aerial or airy meteors (winds), aqueous…
parole.testo: From Middle French météore, from Old French, from Latin meteorum, from Ancient Greek μετέωρον (metéōron), from μετέωρος (metéōros, “raised from the ground, hanging, lofty”), from μετά (metá, “in the midst of, among, between”) (English meta) + ἀείρω (aeírō, “to lift, to heave, to raise up”). The orig

parole.significato: A process by which a task is completed; a way of doing something (followed by the adposition of, to or for before the p…
parole.testo: From Middle French methode, from Latin methodus, from Ancient Greek μέθοδος (méthodos). By surface analysis, met- + -hod. See also -ode and hodo-.

parole.significato: The practice of judging someone's character, or telling their fortune, from studying their face or forehead.
parole.testo: From Middle French metoposcopie, and its source, Late Latin metoposcopia, ultimately from Ancient Greek μέτωπον (métōpon, “forehead”) + -scopy.

parole.significato: A metropolis; the main city of a country or area.
parole.testo: From Middle English metropol, from Middle French metropole (“town with bishop's seat”), from Latin mētropolis. Doublet of metropolis.

parole.significato: An instance of moving to live in another place for a while.
parole.testo: From Middle French migration and its source, Latin migrātiō, from the participle stem of migrō (“to migrate”). Morphologically migrate + -ion.

parole.significato: a native or inhabitant of the ancient city of Miletus in Asia Minor.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French Milesien, and its source Latin Mīlēsius, from Ancient Greek Μιλήσιος (Milḗsios).

parole.significato: Fighting or disposed to fight; belligerent, warlike.
parole.testo: From Middle French militant, from Latin mīlitāns, present participle of mīlitāre (“to serve as a soldier”).

parole.significato: Any of a group of various types of grass or its grains used as food, widely cultivated in the developing world.
parole.testo: From late Middle English, borrowed from Middle French millet; from Latin milium, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, crush”), see also Ancient Greek μελίνη (melínē, “millet”) and Lithuanian málnos (“millet”). Not related to مِلَّة (milla).

parole.significato: The cardinal number 1 000 000: 10⁶; a thousand thousand (1,000²).
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English milioun, from Middle French milion, from Old French millon, from Italian milione (“million”, from mille (“thousand”, from Latin mille) + -one). Compare -illion.

parole.significato: Threatening, menacing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French minatoire, from Late Latin minātōrius. Compare menace.

parole.significato: Favoured, beloved; "pet".
parole.testo: First use appears c. 1490, from Middle French mignon (“lover, royal favourite, darling”), from Old French mignon (“dainty, pleasing, gentle, kind”), from Frankish *minnju (“love, friendship, affection, memory”), from Proto-Germanic *minjō (“affectionate thought, care”), from Proto-Indo-European *men

parole.significato: To lessen or cause to seem to be less.
parole.testo: From Middle English menuse, from Middle French menusier, from Vulgar Latin *minūtiāre.

parole.significato: To attend to (the needs of); to tend; to take care (of); to give aid; to give service.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English mynystren, from Middle French ministrer, from Old French menistrer, ministrer and Latin ministrō, from minister.

parole.significato: Related to a religious minister or ministry.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French ministeriel, equivalent to minister + -ial. Doublet of minstrel and ministerialis.

parole.significato: That diminishes or attenuates
parole.testo: From the late-Middle French minoratif, minorative (“that diminishes or lessens”, of a medicine “mildly laxative”; as a noun “a mild laxative”), from minorer (“to diminish the importance [of]”). Equivalent to minorate (“diminish”, “lessen”) + -ive. Compare the post-Classical (i.e. 9th C.) Latin minōr

parole.significato: The state or condition of being smaller, inferior, or subordinate to something or someone else; lesserness.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English minoritie, from Middle French minorité, and its source Late Latin minōritās, from Latin minor. Morphologically minor + -ity.

parole.significato: By supernatural or uncommon causes, e.g. by a god; that cannot be explained in terms of normal events.
parole.testo: From Middle French miraculeux. Displaced native Old English wundorlīċ.

parole.significato: In a state of misery: very sad, ill, or poor.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French miserable, from Old French, from Latin miserabilis, equivalent to miser + -able.

parole.significato: An actual or alleged wrong that arises from an action; often, the wrongful use of legal authority.
parole.testo: From Middle French mesfaisance.

parole.significato: To despise or hold in contempt; to undervalue.
parole.testo: From Middle French mespriser (verb), mespris (noun).

parole.significato: A strong cold north-west wind in southern France and the Mediterranean.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French mistral, from Occitan. Doublet of magistral.

parole.significato: A reduction or decrease of something harmful or unpleasant.
parole.testo: From Middle French mitigation, from Latin mītigātiō.

parole.significato: The act or process of mixing; the state of being mixed or becoming mixed; a mixture.
parole.testo: From Middle French mixtion, mixion, and its source, Latin mixtiō, from mixtus (“mixed”).

parole.significato: Mizzenmast.
parole.testo: From Middle English mesan, meseyn, myson, from Middle French misaine, modified from Old French migenne (through influence from Italian mezzana), from Old Catalan mitjana, feminine of mitjan, ultimately from Latin medianus. Doublet of mean and median.

parole.significato: The ability to move; capacity for movement.
parole.testo: From Middle French mobilité, and its source, Latin mōbilitās (“mobility”).

parole.significato: Of, or relating to a mode or modus.
parole.testo: From Middle French modal, from Medieval Latin modālis (“pertaining to a mode”), from Latin modus (“mode”). Compare to French, Spanish, and Portuguese modal and Italian modale. By surface analysis, mod(e) + -al.

parole.significato: A person who poses as a subject or visual reference for an artist.
parole.testo: From Middle French modelle, from Old Italian modello, from Vulgar Latin *modellus, diminutive form of modulus (“measure, standard”), diminutive of modus (“measure”); see mode, and compare module, modulus, mould, mold.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being moderate; avoidance of extremes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French [Term?], from Old French moderacion, from Latin moderātiō. By surface analysis, moderate + ion.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a current or recent time and style; not ancient.
parole.testo: From Middle French moderne, from Late Latin modernus; from Latin modo (“just now”), originally ablative of modus (“measure”); hence, by measure, "just now". See also mode.

parole.significato: Not bragging or boasting about oneself or one's achievements; unpretentious, humble.
parole.testo: From Middle French modeste, from Latin modestus.

parole.significato: The quality of being modest; having a limited and not overly high opinion of oneself and one's abilities.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French modestie, from Latin modestia; equivalent to modest + -y.

parole.significato: The act of assessing and prescribing a payment, penalty, price, valuation, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English modificatioune, from Middle French modification and its etymon Latin modificātiō (“a measuring”), from modificāre (“to limit, control, modify”); see modify. By surface analysis, modify + -ication.

parole.significato: To change part of.
parole.testo: From Middle English modifien, from Middle French modifier, from Latin modificare (“to limit, control, regulate, deponent”), from modificari (“to measure off, set bound to, moderate”), from modus (“measure”) + facere (“to make”); see mode.

parole.significato: Modification or regulation of something to achieve an appropriate measure or proportion; (countable) an instance of thi…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English modulacion, modulacioun (“act of making music or singing; harmony; melody, song”), from Middle French modulation (modern French modulation), and directly from its etymon Latin modulātiō (“regular or rhythmical measure, modulation; inflection of tone; (architecture) calculati

parole.significato: Yarn or fabric made from the hair of the angora goat, often as mixed with cotton or other materials.
parole.testo: Earlier mocayre, from Middle French mocayart and Italian mocaiardo, mocaiarro, both from Arabic مُخَيَّر (muḵayyar, “choice”), past participle of خَيَّرَ (ḵayyara, “to choose”). Form influenced by hair through folk etymology. Doublet of moire; compare mockado.

parole.significato: A half.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French moytié, from Old French meitié (“half”) (modern French moitié (“half”)), from Late Latin medietās (“centre, midpoint; half”), from Latin medius (“half; middle”) + -tās (from Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ts (suffix forming nouns indicating a state of being)). Medius is ultima

parole.significato: Momentary, transient.
parole.testo: From Middle French momentané, from Late Latin momentaneus.

parole.significato: The ruler of an absolute monarchy or the head of state of a constitutional monarchy.
parole.testo: From Middle French monarque, from Late Latin monarcha, from Ancient Greek μονάρχης (monárkhēs), variant of μόναρχος (mónarkhos, “sole ruler”), from μόνος (mónos, “only”) + ἀρχός (arkhós, “leader”), equivalent to mono- + -arch. * (butterfly): See monarch butterfly.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to monarchy or to a monarch.
parole.testo: From Middle French monarchique; equivalent to monarch + -ic.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to a monarch or monarchy.
parole.testo: From monarch + -ical, perhaps after Middle French monarchique.

parole.significato: Of or relating to monasteries or monks.
parole.testo: From Middle French monastique, from Late Latin monasticus.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or consisting of money.
parole.testo: From Middle French monétaire, from Late Latin monētārius (“pertaining to money”), from Latin monētārius (“of a mint”), from monēta (“mint, coinage”), from the presence—from 273 BC to AD 84—of the chief Roman mint at the Templum Iunonis Monetae (“Temple of Juno Moneta”), q.v. Doublet of minter.

parole.significato: A long speech by one person in a play; sometimes a soliloquy; other times spoken to other characters.
parole.testo: First attested in c. 1550. Borrowed from Middle French monologue, modeled on dialogue, ultimately from Byzantine Greek μονόλογος (monólogos). By surface analysis, mono- + -logue.

parole.significato: A fight or other contest between two people or forces; a duel; single combat.
parole.testo: From Middle French monomachie, or its source, Latin monomachia. Also mono- + -machy.

parole.significato: An appellation owned by a single winery.
parole.testo: From the Middle French monopole or its etymon the Late Latin monopōlium (“a monopoly”).

parole.significato: An honorific form of address for an eminent person in France, especially under the Ancien Régime.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French monseigneur. Doublet of monsieur and monsignor.

parole.significato: An organism showing abnormal development or deformity.
parole.testo: From Middle English monstruosite, from Middle French monstruosité and its etymon Late Latin mōnstruōsitās, mōnstrōsitās (“monstrousness”), from Latin mōnstruōsus, mōnstrōsus; by surface analysis, monstrous + -ity.

parole.significato: A small mountain, or hillock.
parole.testo: From Middle English [Term?], from Middle French monticule.

parole.significato: That causes disease; sickening, pathogenic.
parole.testo: From Middle French morbifique, or its source, post-classical morbificus, from Latin morbus (“sickness”).

parole.significato: The quality of being mordacious; biting severity, or sarcastic quality.
parole.testo: From Middle French mordacité (whence -acity), from Latin mordācitās (“quality of biting”), from mordāx (“biting, snappish, tart”), from mordeō (“bite, nibble”). Compare French mordacité. See mordacious.

parole.significato: To affect (an animal or person) with catarrh or coldlike illness.
parole.testo: From Middle English morfounden, morefounden (“to take cold”), from Middle French morfondre (“to chill, to cool”), from Franco-Provençal mor, more (“snout”) + Middle French fondre (“to melt”), where the first part comes from Vulgar Latin *murrum (“muzzle, snout”), and the second from Latin fundere. C

parole.significato: A kind of open brimmed helmet used by footsoldiers in the 16th and 17th centuries, having no visor or bevor.
parole.testo: From Middle French morion, from, Spanish morrión, from morra (“upper part of the head”), from morro (“muzzle, snout”), from Vulgar Latin *murrum (“muzzle, snout”). Related to moraine (“an amassment of rocks on a glacier”).

parole.significato: A clasp or fastening used to fasten a cope in the front, usually decorative.
parole.testo: From Middle French mors, from Latin morsus (“bite; clasp”), from mordere (“to bite”).

parole.significato: The act of biting.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English morsure, from Middle French or Anglo-Norman morsure, from Early Medieval Latin morsūra, from mordēre, morsum (“to bite”) + -ūra (“ure”).

parole.significato: A legal agreement in which a borrower pledges real property as collateral for a loan used to purchase or refinance that…
parole.testo: From Middle English morgage and Middle French mortgage, from Anglo-Norman morgage, from Old French mort gage (“dead pledge”), after a translation of judicial Medieval Latin mortuum wadium, with wadium from Frankish *wadi (“wager, pledge”). Compare gage and also wage. So called because rents and prof

parole.significato: The act of mortifying.
parole.testo: From Middle English mortificacioun, mortification, from Middle French mortification and its etymon Latin mortificātiō. By surface analysis, mortify + -ication.

parole.significato: Pertaining to Moses, or the writings and traditions attributed to him.
parole.testo: From Middle French mosaïque, moysaique, and its source, post-classical Latin Mosaicus (5th century), from Latin Moses, ultimately from Biblical Hebrew מֹשֶׁה (mōšê).

parole.significato: A piece of artwork created by placing colored pieces (usually tiles, either regular or irregular in shape) in a pattern…
parole.testo: From Middle French mosaïque, from Italian mosaico, from Medieval Latin musaicum, from Late Latin musivum (opus), from Latin museum, musaeum, probably from Ancient Greek Μουσεῖον (Mouseîon), shrine of the Muses (Μοῦσα (Moûsa)). Doublet of museum.

parole.significato: A place of worship for Muslims, often having at least one minaret; a masjid.
parole.testo: From Middle French mosquée, from Italian moschea, ultimately from Arabic مَسْجِد (masjid, literally “place of prostration”). Doublet of masjid.

parole.significato: Having many mountains; characterized by mountains; of the nature of a mountain; rough (terrain); rocky.
parole.testo: From mountain + -ous after Middle French montagneux, from Late Latin montāniōsus, from montānia, from Latin montem (“mountain”).

parole.significato: A musketeer, especially one of the French royal musketeers of the 17th and 18th centuries, famed for their daring and t…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French mousquetaire. Doublet of musketeer.

parole.significato: A growth of facial hair between the nose and the upper lip.
parole.testo: Used in English since the 16th century. From Middle French moustache from Italian mostaccio, from Early Medieval Latin mustācium, from Byzantine Greek μουστάκιον (moustákion), diminutive of (Doric) Ancient Greek μύσταξ (mústax, “upper lip”), of unknown origin (probably a Pre-Greek substrate). Replac

parole.significato: A thick gluey substance (gum) produced by many plants and some microorganisms.
parole.testo: From Middle English muscilage, mussillage, from Middle French mucilage (“viscous substance found in vegetable material”), from Late Latin mūcilāgō (“musty or moldy juice”). See Greek μούχλα (moúchla, “mold”), and related derivatives, for example mushroom, from *meus- (“mosses, mold, mildew”).

parole.significato: A fine or penalty, especially a pecuniary one.
parole.testo: From Middle French mulcter (“to fine, punish”), from Latin mulcta (“penalty, fine”). Possibly a doublet of milk.

parole.significato: Any shoe with an upper covering the front of the foot but without a back flap or strap, leaving the heel exposed.
parole.testo: From Middle French mule (“backless slipper”), from Medieval Latin mula (“slipper, shoe with a thick sole”), presumably from classical Latin mulleus, the dyed shoe of either the patricians or senators, from mūllus (“red mullet”) + -eus (“-y: forming adjectives”), from Ancient Greek μύλλος (múllos).

parole.significato: A male mule.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French mulet.

parole.significato: The process of computing the sum of an addition with one and the same number a specified number of times (i.e. 4 times…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French, from Old French multiplicacion, from Latin multiplicatio, multiplicationem; ~equivalent to multiplicate + -ion.

parole.significato: Mumming; disguising oneself to perform as a mummer, or to take part in some other festivities or performance.
parole.testo: From Middle French momerie, mommerie, from Old French mommer, from momon. By surface analysis, mummer + -y.

parole.significato: The quality of being munificent; generosity.
parole.testo: From Middle French munificence, from Latin munificentia, from munus (“gift”) + facio (“to make”).

parole.significato: A watch (portable timepiece).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French montre.

parole.significato: wall
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English muren, from Middle French murer, from Old French murer (“to close by a wall”), from Late Latin mūrō, mūrāre, from Latin mūrus (“wall”). Related to German Mauer (“wall”).

parole.significato: The mulberry fruit.
parole.testo: From Middle English murrey, murreye, from Middle French moré, morée, from Latin moratum, morata, from neuter and feminine respectively of moratus (“mulberry-colored”), from morum (“mulberry”) + -atus (“-ate”).

parole.significato: A dreamer; an absent-minded person.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle English musard, from Middle French musard, from muser (“to loiter, trifle”). See muse (intransitive verb).

parole.significato: A black spot like an ermine spot, but without its three specks.
parole.testo: From Middle French mouscheture, from Latin musca (“a fly”).

parole.significato: A contractile form of tissue which animals use to effect movement.
parole.testo: From Middle English muscle, muscule, muskylle, and in part from Middle French muscle, from Latin mūsculus (“a muscle”, literally “little mouse”) because of the mouselike appearance of some muscles, from mūs (“mouse”). Doublet of mussel. More at mouse.

parole.significato: Made up of muscle or muscle tissue; muscular.
parole.testo: From late Middle English, from Middle French musculeux (“composed of muscle”), from Latin mūsculōsus (“muscular, fleshy”), from mūsculus (“a little mouse; a muscle”) + -ōsus (“-ous, -ose”, adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: Of a person: a source of inspiration.
parole.testo: From Middle French muse, from Latin Mūsa, from Ancient Greek Μοῦσα (Moûsa).

parole.significato: A small hole or gap through which a wild animal passes; a muse.
parole.testo: From Middle French mussette, from Old French mussette, diminutive of musse, muce (“a hiding place”).

parole.significato: Any of various small bagpipes having a soft sound, especially with a bellows, which were popular in France in the 17th…
parole.testo: From both of the following: * Late Middle English musette (“type of bagpipe”), from Middle French musette, Old French musette (“type of bagpipe”) (modern French musette), from muse (“bagpipe”) + -ette (diminutive suffix). Muse is derived from muser (“to play the bagpipe; (figuratively) to flatter”),

parole.significato: A kind of firearm formerly carried by the infantry of an army, originally fired by means of a match, or matchlock, for…
parole.testo: First attested around 1210 as a surname, and later in the 1400s as a word for the sparrowhawk (Middle English forms: musket, muskett, muskete (“sparrow hawk”)), from Middle French mousquet, from Old Italian moschetto (a diminutive of mosca (“fly”), from Latin musca) used to refer initially to a spar

parole.significato: A foot soldier armed with a musket.
parole.testo: From Middle French mousquetaire in the late 16th century. By surface analysis, musket + -eer. Doublet of mousquetaire.

parole.significato: Of a bird: to defecate.
parole.testo: From Middle French muetir, probably a shortened form of esmeutir, ultimately from Proto-Germanic.

parole.significato: To mutiny.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French mutiner.

parole.significato: Mutiny, rebellion.
parole.testo: From Middle French mutin (noun), mutiner (verb).

parole.significato: An organized rebellion against a legally constituted authority, especially by seamen against their officers.
parole.testo: From Middle French mutiner.

parole.significato: Having the same relationship, each to each other.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French mutuel, from Latin mūtuus. Displaced native Old English ġemǣne.

parole.significato: Of unknown origin.
parole.testo: From Middle English *misterius (implied in misteriusly), probably partly from Middle French mystérieux and partly from Latin mystērium + -ous. By surface analysis, mystery + -ous.

parole.significato: To interpret (a story etc.) as mythological; to explain the symbolic meaning of.
parole.testo: From mythology + -ize, after Middle French mythologiser.

parole.significato: The collection of myths of a people, concerning the origin of the people, history, deities, ancestors and heroes.
parole.testo: First attested as Middle English in 1412. From Middle French mythologie, from Latin mȳthologia, from Ancient Greek μυθολογία (muthología, “legend”) μυθολογέω (muthologéō, “to tell tales”), from μυθολόγος (muthológos, “legend”), from μῦθος (mûthos, “story”) + λέγω (légō, “to say”). By surface analysi

parole.significato: A shellfish which contains mother-of-pearl.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French nacre, from Medieval Latin nacchara, ultimately derived from Arabic نَقَّارَة (naqqāra). Doublet of nagara, nagada, naqareh, and naker. Also present in nacarat.

parole.significato: Depicted swimming horizontally.
parole.testo: From Middle French noiant, present participle of noier (“to swim”), from Latin natare. Doublet of natant.

parole.significato: Having only its forepart shown, especially if because it is issuing from an ordinary or division of the field. (Compare…
parole.testo: From Middle French naissant (literally “being born”). Doublet of nascent.

parole.significato: Narcissus.
parole.testo: From Middle French narcisse and its etymon Latin narcissus.

parole.significato: Any substance or drug that reduces pain, induces sleep and may alter mood or behaviour; in some contexts, especially in…
parole.testo: From Middle English narcotyk, from Middle French narcotique (from Old French narcotique, noun use of adjective) and directly from Medieval Latin narcōticum, from Ancient Greek ναρκωτῐκόν (narkōtĭkón), neuter of ναρκωτῐκός (narkōtĭkós), from Ancient Greek ναρκόω (narkóō, “to benumb”), from νάρκη (nár

parole.significato: Of, or relating to narcotics.
parole.testo: From Middle French narcotique or German narkotisch and directly from Medieval Latin narcōticus, from Ancient Greek ναρκωτῐκός (narkōtĭkós).

parole.significato: The act of recounting or relating in order the particulars of some action, occurrence, or affair; a narrating.
parole.testo: From Middle French narration, from Old French narracion, from Latin narrātiō. By surface analysis, Latin narr- + -ate + -ion.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a nation or country, especially as a whole; affecting, shared by, or existing throughout all of a nation;…
parole.testo: From Middle French national, corresponding to nation + -al.

parole.significato: The action of naturalizing somebody; act of granting citizenship.
parole.testo: From Middle French naturalisation.

parole.significato: To grant citizenship to someone not born a citizen.
parole.testo: From Middle French naturaliser. By surface analysis, natural + -ize.

parole.significato: A place built to stage a mock sea-battle, or the show performed therein.
parole.testo: From Middle French naumachie and its source, Latin naumachia.

parole.significato: Synonym of nautical.
parole.testo: A borrowing from Middle French nautique (“of or relating to sailors or navigation”) and a learned borrowing from its etymon, Classical Latin nauticus (“of or relating to ships, seafaring”), from Ancient Greek ναυτικός (nautikós), from ναύτης (naútēs, “sailor”) + -ικός (-ikós, adjectival suffix). Com

parole.significato: Of, relating to, or characteristic of sailing, sailors, or the sea.
parole.testo: From Middle French nautique (“of or relating to sailors or navigation”) or its etymon, Classical Latin nauticus (“of or relating to ships, seafaring”), + -al (adjectival suffix). Nauticus is from Ancient Greek ναυτικός (nautikós), from ναύτης (naútēs, “sailor”) + -ικός (-ikós, adjecival suffix). Com

parole.significato: Of or relating to a navy.
parole.testo: From Middle English naval, from Middle French naval, from Latin nāvālis; equivalent to navy + -al.

parole.significato: A kind of small turnip, a variety of Brassica napus.
parole.testo: From Middle French naveau, navel, from Old French naveau, navel, from Medieval Latin nāpellus, a diminutive of Latin nāpus (“turnip, rapeseed, etc”).

parole.significato: Shaped like a boat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French naviculaire, itself borrowed from Late Latin nāviculāris (“boat shaped”), from Latin nāvicula, diminutive of nāvis (“ship”), from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂us.

parole.significato: Capable of being navigated; deep enough and wide enough to afford passage to vessels.
parole.testo: From Middle French navigable, from Latin navigabilis.

parole.significato: The theory, practice and technology of charting a course for a road vehicle, ship, aircraft, or spaceship.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French navigation, from Latin nāvigātiōnem, accusative singular of nāvigātiō (“sailing, navigation”), from nāvigō (“sail”). Morphologically navigate + -ion.

parole.significato: In the form of a cloud or haze; hazy.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English nebulous, from Middle French nebuleus, from Latin nebulōsus (“full of mist, foggy, cloudy”), from nebula (“mist, vapour, cloud”), from Proto-Indo-European *nébʰos (“cloud, vapor, fog, moist, sky”). By surface analysis, nebula + -ous. More at neveling, nuel. Cognates * A

parole.significato: Needy, indigent, destitute, poor.
parole.testo: From necessity + -ous, after Middle French nécessiteux.

parole.significato: Synonym of negro or nigger.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French nègre, from Spanish and Portuguese negro, ultimately from Latin niger. Doublet of negro and noir.

parole.significato: To clean, wash, rinse.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French nettoyer (“to cleanse”).

parole.significato: Not taking sides in a conflict such as war; nonaligned.
parole.testo: From Middle French neutral (compare modern French neutre), from Latin neutrālis. By surface analysis, neuter + -al.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being neutral; the condition of being unengaged in contests between others; state of taking no…
parole.testo: From Middle French neutralité, from Medieval Latin neutralitas. Morphologically neutral + -ity.

parole.significato: Someone who hides their faith or belief in something; a secret adherent.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French Nicodemite, corresponding to Nicodemus + -ite, after a Pharisee in the Gospel of John who secretly comes to Jesus for instruction while outwardly remaining a pious Jew.

parole.significato: A nest of pheasants.
parole.testo: Uncertain; possibly from Middle French nid (modern French nid (“nest”)), or its etymon Latin nīdus (“nest”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nisdós (“nest”)). Doublet of nest.

parole.significato: A black person; a person of black African descent.
parole.testo: Alteration of earlier neger, from Middle French nègre (“a black person”), from Spanish negro. Ultimately from Latin niger (“black”), thus a doublet of negro and noir. The expected Modern English pronunciation would be with /iː/; compare neger. The modern pronunciation with /ɪ/ may be due to influenc

parole.significato: Pertaining to or composed of nitre; having the properties of nitre, bitter.
parole.testo: From Middle French nitreux, and its source, Latin nitrōsus (“nitrose”). Doublet of nitroso. By surface analysis, nitro- + -ous.

parole.significato: Of a person, creature, group, or species, primarily active during the night.
parole.testo: From Middle French nocturnal, from Latin nocturnālis (“nocturnal”), from Latin nocturnus (“nocturnal”), from Latin nox (“night”), from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts (“night”). Cognates include Ancient Greek νύξ (núx), Sanskrit नक्ति (nákti), Old English niht (English night) and Proto-Slavic *noťь.

parole.significato: A member of a society or class who herd animals from pasture to pasture with no fixed home.
parole.testo: From Middle French nomade, from Latin Nomas (“wandering shepherd”), from Ancient Greek νομάς (nomás, “roaming, wandering, esp. to find pasture”), from Ancient Greek νομός (nomós, “pasture”). Compare Numidia.

parole.significato: A point halfway between the fess point (centre of the shield) and the middle base (bottom) point of an escutcheon.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French nombril.

parole.significato: An act or instance of nominating.
parole.testo: From Middle English nominacion, nomination, from Middle French nominacion and its etymon Latin nōminātiō, from the verb nōminō (“to name; to nominate”). By surface analysis, nominate + -ion.

parole.significato: Unequalled, unrivalled; unique.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English non-parail (“unparalleled, nonpareil”) [and other forms], from Middle French nonpareille, nonpareil (“unparalleled”) (obsolete), from non- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + pareil (“alike, like, same”). Pareil is derived from Old French pareil, from Late Latin pāriculus (“equal; like

parole.significato: A V-shaped cut.
parole.testo: Recorded since 1577, probably a rebracketing of an otch, from Middle French oche (“notch”), itself from the Old French verb ochier (“to notch”), of uncertain origin, but possibly related to French hocher and English nick (“small cut, notch”).

parole.significato: The act of observing; perception.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French notice, from the Latin nōtitia. Doublet of notitia.

parole.significato: The act of notifying.
parole.testo: From Middle French notification, from Old French notificacion, from Latin nōtificātiō.

parole.significato: An infamous or notorious condition or reputation.
parole.testo: Derived from Middle French notoriété, from Medieval Latin nōtōrietās, from nōtōrius, from nōtus (“known”), perfect passive participle of nōscō (“get to know”). By surface analysis, notorious + -ety.

parole.significato: The act of nourishing or the state of being nourished.
parole.testo: From Middle English norisshement, from Middle French, from Old French norissement, from norrir, equivalent to nourish + -ment.

parole.significato: An innovation; a novelty.
parole.testo: Inherited from the Middle English novitē (“an innovative practice”), borrowed from Middle French novité (“novelty, change, innovation”), from the Latin novitās (“newness, novelty; rareness, strangeness; newness of rank; reformation”); cognate with the Italian novità, the Portuguese novidade, the Rom

parole.significato: Harmful; of the nature of a nuisance.
parole.testo: From Middle English nusant, nuysande, from Middle French nuisant, present participle of nuire (“to harm”). Doublet of nocent.

parole.significato: A non-existent or empty value or set of values.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French nul, from Latin nūllus.

parole.significato: The state of being null, or void, or invalid.
parole.testo: From Middle French nullité and its etymon Medieval Latin nūllitās, from Latin nūllus. By surface analysis, null + -ity.

parole.significato: The entrails of a deer or other animal, used for food.
parole.testo: From Middle French nombles (“loin of meat”), alteration (with dissimilation) of Old French and Anglo-Norman lumbles (“loins”), from Latin lumbulus, diminutive of lumbus (“loin”).

parole.significato: Oral; not written.
parole.testo: From Middle English nuncupatif, nuncupatife, from Middle French nuncupatif and its etymon Latin nuncupātīvus (“nominal”).

parole.significato: The nape of the neck.
parole.testo: From Middle French nuque, nuche, from Medieval Latin nucha, from Arabic نُخَاع (nuḵāʕ). Doublet of nucha.

parole.significato: The organic process by which an organism assimilates food and uses it for growth and maintenance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French nutrition, from Old French nutricion, from Latin nutritio.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to nutrition.
parole.testo: From Middle French nutritif, from Late Latin nūtritīvus, from the participle stem of Latin nūtriō (“to suckle”).

parole.significato: A lighthouse.
parole.testo: From Middle French obeliscolychnie (in Rabelais), from Ancient Greek ὀβελισκολύχνιον (obeliskolúkhnion, “spit used as a lamp-holder”), from ὀβελίσκος (obelískos, “obelisk”) + λυχνίον (lukhníon, “lamp-stand”).

parole.significato: A tall, square, tapered, stone monolith topped with a pyramidal point, frequently used as a monument.
parole.testo: From Middle French obelisque, from Latin obeliscus (“obelisk”), from Ancient Greek ὀβελίσκος (obelískos), diminutive of ὀβελός (obelós, “needle”). Compare obelus.

parole.significato: The act of objecting.
parole.testo: From Middle French objection, from Old French objeccion, from Latin obiectio. Equivalent to object + -ion.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a material object, actual existence or reality.
parole.testo: From Middle English obgectyf, from Middle French objectif and its etymon Medieval Latin obiectīvus. By surface analysis, object + -ive.

parole.significato: Not erect or perpendicular; not parallel to, or at right angles from, the base.
parole.testo: From Middle French oblique, from Latin oblīquus (also spelled oblīcus) (“slanting, sideways, indirect, envious”).

parole.significato: The quality of being oblique in direction, deviating from the horizontal or vertical; or the angle created by such a de…
parole.testo: From Middle French obliquité, from Latin oblīquitās, from oblīquus (“oblique”). Corresponding to oblique + -ity.

parole.significato: Abusive language.
parole.testo: From Middle English obloqui, obloquie, obloquy, from Middle French obloquie and its etymon Late Latin obloquium (“contradiction”), from Latin obloquor (“speak against, contradict”). By surface analysis, ob- + -loquy.

parole.significato: Offensive to standards of decency or morality.
parole.testo: From Middle French obscene (modern French obscène (“indecent, obscene”)), and from its etymon Latin obscēnus, obscaenus (“inauspicious; ominous; disgusting, filthy; offensive, repulsive; indecent, lewd, obscene”). The further etymology is uncertain, but may be from ob- (prefix meaning ‘towards’) + c

parole.significato: Darkness; the absence of light.
parole.testo: From Middle English obscurite, obscuryte, from Middle French obscurité and its etymon Latin obscūritās. By surface analysis, obscure + -ity.

parole.significato: The act of observing, and the fact of being observed (see observance)
parole.testo: From Middle English observacion, borrowed from Middle French observacion. Also a borrowing from French observation and a learned borrowing from Latin observātiō(n-). Morphologically observe + -ation.

parole.significato: An observer.
parole.testo: From Middle French observateur, from Latin observator, from the participle stem of observare.

parole.significato: To notice or view, especially carefully or with attention to detail.
parole.testo: From Middle French observer, from Old French observer, from Latin observō (“to watch”), from ob- (“before”) + servō (“to keep”), from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to guard”). Cognate with Gothic 𐍃𐌰𐍂𐍅𐌰 (sarwa, “weapons, armour”), Old English searu (“device”).

parole.significato: Disparagement, the belittling of someone or something; slander.
parole.testo: From Middle French obtrectacion and its source, Latin obtrectātiō (“disparagement”), from the participle stem of obtrectāre.

parole.significato: A favorable opportunity; a convenient or timely chance.
parole.testo: From Middle English occasioun, from Middle French occasion, from Old French occasiun, from Latin occāsiōnem, noun of action from perfect passive participle occāsus, from verb occidō, from prefix ob- (“down", "away”) + verb cadō (“fall”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or situated in, the occident, or west; western.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French occidental, from Latin occidentalis, equivalent to occident + -al.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or located within or near the occiput (back of the head) or the occipital bone.
parole.testo: Borrowing from Middle French occipital, from Medieval Latin occipitālis, from occiput (“the back of the head, occiput”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix), equivalent of occiput + -al. Doublet of occipitalis.

parole.significato: A person who occupies an office or a position.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French occupant (present participle of occuper) or Latin occupāns, occupantis (present participle of occupō). By surface analysis, occupy + -ant.

parole.significato: An activity or task with which one occupies oneself; usually specifically the productive activity, service, trade, or c…
parole.testo: From Middle English occupacioun, borrowed from Middle French occupacion, occupation, from Latin occupātiō, occupātiōnis, from occupō (“occupy, seize”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“to seize, grab”). By surface analysis, occupy + -ation.

parole.significato: One who occupies, particularly with respect to a foreign government controlling the territory of another.
parole.testo: From Middle English occupier, occupiour, from occupien + -er (equivalent to occupy + -er) or Middle French occupier, occupiour.

parole.significato: To happen or take place.
parole.testo: Originally "meet (in argument)", borrowed from Middle French occurrer, from Latin occurrō (“run to meet, run against, befall, present itself”) from prefix ob- (“against”) + verb currō (“run, hurry, move”).

parole.significato: An actual instance when a situation occurs; an event or happening.
parole.testo: From Middle French occurrence, from Medieval Latin occurrentia. Morphologically occur + -ence.

parole.significato: Current, actual, occurring.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French occurrent and its source, Latin occurrēns.

parole.significato: A line behind which a player's front foot must be placed when throwing a dart.
parole.testo: Possibly from Middle French oche (“notch”), from Old French ocher, ochier (“to make a notch in; to notch”), which, according to Partridge, could be related to French hocher and English nick (“small cut, notch”).

parole.significato: Mob rule; government by the masses; mobocracy.
parole.testo: From Middle French ochlocratie, from Ancient Greek ὀχλοκρατία (okhlokratía), from ὄχλος (ókhlos, “multitude, crowd”) + κράτος (krátos, “power”). Equivalent to ochlo- + -cracy.

parole.significato: To grant (a privilege etc, by a government etc).
parole.testo: From Middle English octroy, from Middle French octroyer, from Old French otroiier, from Latin auctōrizō. Doublet of authorize.

parole.significato: A short poetical composition proper to be set to music or sung; a lyric poem; especially, now, a poem characterized by…
parole.testo: From Middle French ode, from Late Latin ōda, from Ancient Greek ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”). Doublet of Aoede.

parole.significato: To hurt the feelings of; to displease; to make angry; to insult.
parole.testo: From Middle French offendre, from Latin offendō (“strike, blunder, commit an offense”), from ob- (“against”) + *fendō (“strike”).

parole.significato: Causing offense; arousing a visceral reaction of disgust, anger, hatred, sadness, or indignation.
parole.testo: From Middle French offensif, from offendre + -if by analogy with défensif. Offendre is from Latin offendere (“to offend”); see offend.

parole.significato: The sense of smell; the detection of airborne molecules.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French olfaction /olefaction, from Latin olfactus, perfect passive participle of olfaciō (“to smell (transitive)”) + -tion.

parole.significato: Olibanum.
parole.testo: From Middle French oliban. Doublet of olibanum.

parole.significato: Imposing or constituting a physical, mental, or figurative load which can be borne only with effort; burdensome.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English onerous, borrowed from Middle French onereux, from Old French onereus, a learned borrowing from Latin onerosus, from onus (“burden”) + -ōsus. Compare exonerate.

parole.significato: Effectual or important.
parole.testo: From Middle English operative, operatyfe, from Middle French operatif (modern French opératif) or its etymon Latin operātīvus. By surface analysis, operate + -ive.

parole.significato: Conjectural; expressing an opinion rather than a fact.
parole.testo: From opine + -ate + -ive. Middle French opinatif, and its source, Late Latin opinativus, from the participle stem of Latin opīnārī.

parole.significato: To express an opinion; to state as an opinion; to suppose, consider (that).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French opiner, from Latin opīnor (“to hold as an opinion”), from *opīnus (“thinking, expecting”), only in negative nec-opīnus (“not expecting”) and in-opīnus (“not expected”); akin to optō (“to choose, desire”), and to apīscor (“to obtain”); see optate and opt.

parole.significato: A chance for advancement, progress or profit.
parole.testo: From opportune + -ity, from Middle French opportunité, from Latin opportūnitās.

parole.significato: Causing opprobrium; offensive and shameful.
parole.testo: From Middle English opprobrious, from Middle French opprobrieux and its etymon Late Latin opprobriōsus.

parole.significato: To contradict or controvert; to oppose; to challenge or question the truth or validity of a given statement.
parole.testo: From Middle French oppugner Latin oppugno (“fight against, to attack, assail, assault, storm, besiege, war with”).

parole.significato: Expressing a wish or a choice.
parole.testo: From Middle French optatif, from Late Latin optātīvus, a calque of Ancient Greek εὐκτική (euktikḗ, “related to wishing”), from Latin optātus, past participle of optāre.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to the eye or to vision.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French optique or Medieval Latin opticus, from Ancient Greek ὀπτῐκός (optĭkós, “of or for sight”), from ὀπτός (optós, “visible”) + -ῐκός (-ĭkós, “-ic”, adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: A small or petty work.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French opuscule, from Latin opusculum, diminutive of opus. Compare opuscle, opusculum. Equivalent to opus + -cule.

parole.significato: The gold or yellow tincture on a coat of arms.
parole.testo: From late Middle English or (“gold”), borrowed from Middle French or (“yellow”), from Old French or, from Latin aurum (“gold”). Doublet of aurum.

parole.significato: Of or relating to an oracle.
parole.testo: From Middle French oraculaire.

parole.significato: An evergreen tree of the genus Citrus such as Citrus sinensis which yields oranges (the fruit).
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English orenge, orange, from Old French pome orenge (“fruit orange”), influenced by the place name Orange (which is from Gaulish and unrelated to the word for the fruit and colour) and by Old Occitan auranja and calqued from Old Italian melarancio, melarancia, compound of mela

parole.significato: Any of several large, ferocious sea creatures, now especially the killer whale.
parole.testo: From Middle French orque, Italian orca, and their source, Latin orca (“type of whale”). Doublet of orca.

parole.significato: The act of ordaining or the state of being ordained.
parole.testo: From Middle French ordination, from Old French ordinacion, from Latin ordinatio.

parole.significato: Dung, excrement.
parole.testo: From Middle English ordure, ordure, borrowed from Middle French ordure and Anglo-Norman ordure, ordeur(e), ordor(e), ordour from Old French ordure (“dirt, filth, refuse; dung, excrement; moral filth”) (modern French ordure), from ord (“filthy”) + -ure (suffix forming nouns describing the results of

parole.significato: The work or trade of a goldsmith.
parole.testo: From Middle English orfeovre, from Middle French orfaverie, orfavrerie (modern orfèvrerie).

parole.significato: Non-Oxford British English and Australian standard spelling of organization.
parole.testo: From Middle French organisation, equivalent to organise + -ation.

parole.significato: Non-Oxford British standard spelling of organize.
parole.testo: From Middle French organiser. By surface analysis, organ + -ise.

parole.significato: A musician who plays the organ.
parole.testo: From Middle French organiste, from Medieval Latin organista. By surface analysis, organ + -ist.

parole.significato: The quality of being organized.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French organisation, from Medieval Latin organizātiō; by surface analysis, organize + -ation.

parole.significato: To arrange in working order.
parole.testo: From Middle English organizen, organysen, partly from Middle French organiser and partly from its etymon, Medieval Latin organizō, from Latin organum (“organ”). By surface analysis, organ + -ize.

parole.significato: A mouth or aperture, such as of a tube, pipe, etc.; an opening.
parole.testo: From Middle French, from Old French, from Late Latin ōrificium (“an opening, literally the making of a mouth”), compound of ōs (“mouth”) + faciō (“to make”).

parole.significato: Any of various colourful passerine birds, New World orioles of the genus Icterus (family Icteridae) and Old World oriol…
parole.testo: A borrowing from Middle French oriol, from Old French oriol, from Latin aureolus, diminutive of aureus (“golden”). Doublet of aureole. First use appears c. 1776 in the writings of Thomas Pennant.

parole.significato: Conforming to the accepted, established, or traditional doctrines of a given faith, religion, or ideology.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English orthodoxe, from Middle French orthodoxe and its etymon Late Latin orthodoxus, from Ancient Greek ὀρθόδοξος (orthódoxos), from ὀρθός (orthós, “straight”) + δόξα (dóxa, “opinion”). Displaced native Old English wuldorlīċ.

parole.significato: Of two objects, at right angles; perpendicular to each other.
parole.testo: From Middle French orthogonal, in turn from Medieval Latin orthogōnālis and Latin orthogōnius (“right-angled”), ultimately from Ancient Greek ὀρθογώνιος (orthogṓnios, “rectangular”). By surface analysis, ortho- + -gon + -al.

parole.significato: A small European migratory bunting (Emberiza hortulana), once eaten whole as a delicacy.
parole.testo: From Middle French hortolan (“gardener”), from Latin hortulānus (“gardener”). Doublet of hortulan.

parole.significato: Either of the horn-like protuberances on the heads of giraffes and male okapi. Some extinct species in the family bore…
parole.testo: From Latin os (“bone”) and Middle French cone, from Latin cōnus (“cone, wedge, peak”), from Ancient Greek κῶνος (kônos, “cone, spinning top, pine cone”).

parole.significato: Gypaetus barbatus, the bearded vulture, the diet of which is almost exclusively bone marrow.
parole.testo: From Middle French ossifrage, from Latin ossifraga (“osprey”), ossifragus (“osprey”), from ossifragus (“bone breaking”).

parole.significato: The act of presenting an ostensive definition.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French ostension, in turn from Latin ostensiō, ostensiōnem.

parole.significato: Apparently true, but not necessarily; ostensible
parole.testo: From Middle French ostensif and its etymon Late Latin ostēnsīvus.

parole.significato: To make an ambitious display of; to exhibit or show boastingly; to ostentate.
parole.testo: From Middle French ostenter (“to make an ostentatious display of”), or directly from its etymon Latin ostentāre (“to exhibit, present, show; to show off”), frequentative of ostendere (“to exhibit, show”), from ob- (prefix meaning ‘against; towards’) + tendere (“to extend, stretch; to distend”) (from

parole.significato: A portent, a token.
parole.testo: From Middle French ostente (“amazing or marvellous thing; prodigy, wonder”) or directly from its etymon Latin ostentum (“portent”), from ostendere (“to exhibit, show”); see further at etymology 1. The plural form ostenta is from Latin ostenta.

parole.significato: Ambitious display; vain show; display intended to excite admiration or applause.
parole.testo: Originated 1425–75 from late Middle English ostentacioun, borrowed from Middle French ostentation and its etymon Latin ostentātiō, ostentātiōnem, equivalent to ostentātus (past participle of ostentāre, to display or exhibit), frequentative of ostendere (“to present, display”) + -iōn. By surface anal

parole.significato: The state or quality of being otiose.
parole.testo: From otiose + -ity, from Middle French ociosité, from Latin otiositas, from Latin otiosus + -itas (“-ity”).

parole.significato: A member of the Ottoman dynasty.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French Ottoman (“Osman”), borrowed from Italian Ottomano, borrowed from Arabic عُثْمَان (ʕuṯmān). Doublet of Osman and Uthman.

parole.significato: An avoirdupois ounce, weighing ¹⁄₁₆ of an avoirdupois pound, or 28.349523125 grams.
parole.testo: From Middle English ounce, unce, from Middle French once, from Latin ū̆ncia (“Roman ounce, various similar units”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *óynos (“one”). Doublet of a, one, inch, uncia, onça, onza, oka, ouguiya, and awqiyyah.

parole.significato: A large wild feline, such as a lynx or cougar.
parole.testo: From Middle French once, from Old French lonce (“lynx”), by false division (the l was thought to be the article), from Italian lonza, ultimately from Ancient Greek λύγξ (lúnx, “lynx”). Doublet of onza and lynx.

parole.significato: Calm, peaceful.
parole.testo: From Middle French pacifique.

parole.significato: To bring peace to (a place or situation), by ending (or suppressing) war, fighting, violence, anger or agitation.
parole.testo: From Middle French pacifier, from Latin pāx (“peace”) + faciō (“to do, make”). Cognate with pay and peacify.

parole.significato: An agreement; a compact; a covenant.
parole.testo: From Middle English pact, from Middle French pacte, from Old French, and its etymon Latin pactum (“something agreed upon”), from pacīscī (“to agree”).

parole.significato: To mark or number the pages of, as a book or manuscript.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French page, from Latin pāgina, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ǵ-. Doublet of pagina.

parole.significato: A chain or rope used to attach the shank of an anchor to the side of a ship when not in use.
parole.testo: Probably from Middle French pendeur.

parole.significato: Rebirth; regeneration.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French, French palingénésie, from Late Latin palingenesia: see further at palingenesis.

parole.significato: An ode or other poem in which the author retracts something said in an earlier poem; (loosely) a recantation.
parole.testo: From Middle French palinod, from Latin palinōdia (“palinode, recantation”), from Ancient Greek παλινῳδία (palinōidía, “palinode”), from πάλιν (pálin, “again”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”).

parole.significato: A 17th-century game in which a ball was driven along an alley and through a hoop using a mallet.
parole.testo: From Middle French pallemaille, pale-maille, from Italian pallamaglio (“ball-hammer”), from Italian palla (“ball”) and maglio (“hammer”).

parole.significato: A narrow vertical stripe, narrower than a pale. Diminutive of pale.
parole.testo: Said to be from Middle English *palet, from Middle French *palet, from Middle French pal (“pale”), ultimately from Latin palla (“a strip of cloth”).

parole.significato: A beggar or vagrant, especially a professional one; (earlier especially) a lecher.
parole.testo: From Middle English payllart (1484), Middle French paillard, from Middle French paille (“straw”).

parole.significato: Fornication, lechery.
parole.testo: From palliard + -ise, after Middle French paillardise.

parole.significato: The alleviation of a disease's symptoms without a cure; temporary relief.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French palliation, from Latin palliare (“to cloak; to conceal”), from Latin pallium (“cloak”). By surface analysis, palliate + -ion.

parole.significato: Serving to palliate; serving to extenuate or mitigate.
parole.testo: From Middle French palliatif, from New Latin *palliātīvus, from Medieval Latin palliō (“to cloak”), from Latin pallium (“a cloak”).

parole.significato: Capable of being touched, felt or handled; touchable, tangible.
parole.testo: From Middle French palpable and its source, Latin palpābilis, which is from palpō (“to touch softly”) + -bilis.

parole.significato: An abnormal beating of the heart that may be perceived by the patient, a result of excitement, exertion, or illness.
parole.testo: From Middle French palpitation, from Latin palpitatio.

parole.significato: A small, brief printed work, consisting either of a folded sheet of paper, or several sheets bound together into a book…
parole.testo: The noun is derived from Late Middle English pamflet, pamphilet (“short written text; small book; tract”) [and other forms], from Middle French Pamphilet (compare Late Latin (Anglo-Latin) pamfletus, panfletus, paunflettus (“short written text”), Old French Panfilès), a popular shorthand for the 12th

parole.significato: To cause (someone) to feel panic (“overwhelming fear or fright”); also, to frighten (someone) into acting hastily.
parole.testo: The adjective is borrowed from Middle French panique, a word itself borrowed from Ancient Greek πανικός (panikós, “pertaining to Pan”); Pan, the Greek god of fields and woods, was believed to be the source of mysterious sounds that caused contagious, groundless fear in herds and crowds, or in people

parole.significato: A membrane of tissue in the body of a human or animal.
parole.testo: From Middle French pannicle, and its source, Late Latin panniculus (“membrane”), from Latin panniculus (“small rag”), from pannus (“cloth”).

parole.significato: A cultivated flowering plant, derived by hybridization within species Viola tricolor.
parole.testo: From Middle French pensée (“thought”), as the plant resembles someone that is in deep thought, with a lowered head. Doublet of pensée.

parole.significato: A slipper.
parole.testo: From Middle English pantuflis pl, pantuiffillis pl, from Middle French pantoufle (“slipper”), of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: A Roman Catholic, especially one whose loyalties are seen to be with the papacy in Rome.
parole.testo: From Middle French papiste, from Latin pāpa (“pope”).

parole.significato: An apparently self-contradictory statement, which can only be true if it is false, and vice versa.
parole.testo: From Middle French paradoxe, from Latin paradoxum, from Ancient Greek παράδοξος (parádoxos, “unexpected, strange”).

parole.significato: A person of preeminent qualities, who acts as a pattern or model for others.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French paragon, paragone, from Old Italian paragone, from paragonare (“to test on a touchstone”), perhaps from Ancient Greek παρακονᾶν (parakonân, “to sharpen, whet”), from παρά- (pará-) + ἀκόνη (akónē, “whetstone, sharpening stone”), from ἀκή (akḗ, “point, edge”) (from Proto-In

parole.significato: A passage in text that starts on a new line, the first line sometimes being indented, and usually marks a change of top…
parole.testo: From Middle English paragraf, from Middle French paragraphe from Latin paragraphus (“sign for start of a new section of discourse”), from Ancient Greek παράγραφος (parágraphos), from παρά (pará, “beside”) and γράφω (gráphō, “to write”). Doublet of paragraphos.

parole.significato: Any of various species of small parrot primarily of tropical regions.
parole.testo: From Middle French perroquet, probably a diminutive form of the personal name Pierre; some variant forms perhaps via Italian parrocchetto, Spanish periquito.

parole.significato: An apparent shift in the position of two stationary objects relative to each other as viewed by an observer, due to a c…
parole.testo: From Middle French parallaxe, from Ancient Greek παράλλαξις (parállaxis, “alteration”) from παραλλάσσω (parallássō, “to cause to alternate”) from ἀλλάσσω (allássō, “to alter”) from ἄλλος (állos, “other”). See also para- and allo-.

parole.significato: Equally distant from one another at all points.
parole.testo: From Middle French parallèle and its etymon Latin parallēlus, parallēlos. The verb is from the noun. See also para- and allo-.

parole.significato: A fallacious argument or illogical conclusion, especially one committed by mistake, or believed by the speaker to be lo…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French paralogisme, from Late Latin paralogismus, from Ancient Greek παραλογισμός (paralogismós).

parole.significato: A friend of the bridegroom; a best man; a bridesmaid.
parole.testo: From Middle French paranymphe, from Latin paranymphus, from Ancient Greek παράνυμφος (paránumphos, “friend of bridegroom”), from παρα- (para-, “para-”) + νύμφη (númphē, “bride”).

parole.significato: A low protective wall.
parole.testo: From Middle French parapet, from Italian parapetto.

parole.significato: Synonym of paraphernalia (“married woman’s property besides her dowry”).
parole.testo: From Middle French parapharnelz. By surface analysis, paraphernal + -s. Attested since the early 1500s, whereas the adjective paraphernal since the late 1700s.

parole.significato: A restatement of a text in different words, often to clarify meaning or from memory rather than verbatim.
parole.testo: From Middle French paraphrase, from Latin paraphrasis, from Ancient Greek παράφρασις (paráphrasis), equivalent to para- + phrase. Doublet of paraphrasis.

parole.significato: An organism that lives on or in another organism of a different species, deriving benefit from living on or in that oth…
parole.testo: From Middle French parasite, from Latin parasitus, from Ancient Greek παράσιτος (parásitos, “person who eats at the table of another”), from noun use of adjective meaning "feeding beside", from παρά (pará, “beside”) + σῖτος (sîtos, “food”).

parole.significato: Pre-eminently; first.
parole.testo: From Middle French paravant, from par + avant.

parole.significato: To vomit, spew out.
parole.testo: From Middle French par- + brake.

parole.significato: The identity and nature of one's parents, and in particular, the legitimacy of one's birth.
parole.testo: From Middle French, from Old French parentage.

parole.significato: Of or relating to a parent.
parole.testo: From Middle French parental, from Latin parentālis, from parens (“parent”).

parole.significato: A native, citizen and/or inhabitant of Paris, France
parole.testo: From Middle English Parisien, perisien, from Middle French parisien, from Medieval Latin parisiānus. By surface analysis, Paris + -ian.

parole.significato: Equality; comparability of strength or intensity.
parole.testo: From Middle French parité, from Late Latin paritās, from Latin pār (“equal”). Equivalent to pari- + -ty.

parole.significato: Parley; talk.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English parlen (“to speak”), from Middle French parler, from Old French parler, from Late Latin parabolō.

parole.significato: A hard, full-fat Italian cheese from Parma or its neighboring province Reggio Emilia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French parmesan, from an earlier Vulgar Latin *parmēsānus, restructuring of Latin parmēnsis (from Latin Parma). Compare Italian parmigiano, Catalan parmesà, Portuguese parmesão, Sicilian parmisanu, Spanish parmesano

parole.significato: Word of mouth.
parole.testo: from Middle French parole, from Latin parabola, from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ). Doublet of parable.

parole.significato: To release (a prisoner) on the understanding that s/he checks in regularly and obeys the law.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French parole (“word, formal promise”), from Old French parole, from Late Latin parabola (“speech”), from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ). Doublet of parabola, parable, and palaver.

parole.significato: A period (especially one of several recurring periods) during the course of an illness when symptoms worsen; a sudden a…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English paroxism, paroxisme (“period of worsening of a disease, attack; sudden recurrent fever”), from Middle French paroxisme, paroxysme, and Old French peroxime (“period of worsening of a disease; bout of fever or illness”) (modern French paroxysme), and from their etymon Late Lat

parole.significato: Someone who kills a relative, especially a parent.
parole.testo: From Middle French parricide, from Latin parricīda, of uncertain origin, perhaps from pār (“equal”).

parole.significato: The killing of a relative, especially a parent.
parole.testo: From Middle French parricide, from Latin parricīdium, of uncertain origin, perhaps from pār (“equal”).

parole.significato: A kind of bird, many species of which are colorful and able to mimic human speech, of the order Psittaciformes or (narr…
parole.testo: First attested in 1525. From Middle French perrot, either a diminutive of Pierre or a shortened form of perroquet (whence also parakeet). Compare French pierrot and Occitan parrat. A number of origins have been suggested for perroquet, such as Spanish periquito and Italian parrocchetto. The relation

parole.significato: A part, portion or share.
parole.testo: From Middle French partage, from partir (“to share”).

parole.significato: Preference, bias in favor of, tendency.
parole.testo: From Middle English parcialite, parcialtee, parcyalte, partialte, percialite, from Middle French partialité and its etymon Medieval Latin partiālitās. Doublet of partialitas.

parole.significato: One who participates.
parole.testo: From stem of particip(ate) + -ant, borrowed from Middle French participant, from Latin participāns, present participle of participō; see participate. Displaced native Old English dǣlnimend (literally “part taker”).

parole.significato: The act of participating, of taking part in something.
parole.testo: From Middle English participacioun, from Middle French [Term?], from Old French participacion, from Late Latin participatiō. By surface analysis, participate + -ion.

parole.significato: A very small piece of matter, a fragment; especially, the smallest possible part of something.
parole.testo: From Middle French particule, and its source, Latin particula (“small part, particle”), diminutive of pars (“part, piece”). Semantically displaced native Old English grot whence modern English groat.

parole.significato: A particular thing.
parole.testo: From Middle French particularité (“part of a whole; something particular, particularity”) (modern French particularité), and from its etymon Late Latin particularitas (“fact or quality of being particular; something particular, particularity”), from Latin particulāris (“particular; partial”) + -tās

parole.significato: A lampoon, originally as published in public; a satire or libel on someone.
parole.testo: From Middle French, from Italian pasquinata, from Pasquino, name given to a statue in Rome on which lampoons were posted.

parole.significato: Being subjected to an action without producing a reaction.
parole.testo: From Middle English passyf, passyve, from Middle French, French passif, from Latin passivus (“serving to express the suffering of an action; in late Latin literally capable of suffering or feeling”), from passus, past participle of pati (“to suffer”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₁- (“to

parole.significato: Something which amuses, and serves to make time pass agreeably.
parole.testo: From earlier passtime, pass-time, from Middle English passe tyme, passetyme, calque of Middle French passetemps.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to shepherds or herders of other livestock.
parole.testo: From Middle French, Old French pastoral, from Latin pāstōrālis, from pāstor (“shepherd”), + adjective suffix -ālis.

parole.significato: A pasture; land that is used for pasture.
parole.testo: From Middle French pasturage (modern French pâturage). By surface analysis, pasture + -age.

parole.significato: Fatherhood, the state or quality of being a father.
parole.testo: From Middle French paternité, from Old French, from Latin paternitās (“paternity”), from paternus (“of or pertaining to a father, paternal”) + -itās, from pater (“father”).

parole.significato: Arousing pity, sympathy, or compassion; exciting pathos.
parole.testo: From Middle French pathétique, from Latin patheticus, from Ancient Greek παθητικός (pathētikós, “subject to feeling, capable of feeling, impassioned”), from παθητός (pathētós, “one who has suffered, subject to suffering”), from πάσχω (páskhō, “to suffer”). By surface analysis, path- + -etic.

parole.significato: Willing to wait if necessary; not losing one's temper while waiting.
parole.testo: From Middle English pacient, from Middle French patient, from Old French pacient, from Latin patiens, present participle of patior (“to suffer, endure”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₁- (“to hate, hurt”).

parole.significato: A patriarchal system or community.
parole.testo: From Middle French patriarcat, from Old French patriarcat, from Medieval Latin patriarchatus, from Ancient Greek πατριάρχης (patriárkhēs, “patriarch”).
