parole.significato: Having extended wings as if flying.
parole.testo: From Middle French volant, present participle of voler (“to fly”), from Latin volāre.

parole.significato: Evaporating or vaporizing readily under normal conditions.
parole.testo: From Middle French volatile, from Latin volātilis (“flying; swift; temporary; volatile”), from volō (“to fly”).

parole.significato: The simultaneous firing of a number of missiles or bullets; the projectiles so fired.
parole.testo: From Middle French volée (“flight”), from Vulgar Latin volta, from Late Latin volatus.

parole.significato: Turning or whirling; winding.
parole.testo: From Middle French volubile, from Latin volūbilis (“rolling”), from volvō (“to roll”). Doublet of voluble.

parole.significato: Fluent or having a ready flow of speech.
parole.testo: From Middle French volubile, from Latin volūbilis (“rolling”), from volvō (“roll”).

parole.significato: voluptuousness
parole.testo: From Middle English voluptuosite, voluptuositee, voluptuostee, voluptuosyte, voluptuouste, from Middle French voluptuosité; compare Medieval Latin voluptuōsitas. By surface analysis, voluptuous + -osity.

parole.significato: Characterized or marked by full, generous, pleasurable sensation.
parole.testo: From Middle French voluptueux, from Latin voluptuōsus (“delightful”), from voluptās (“pleasure, delight”), from volup (“with pleasure”).

parole.significato: The state of being voracious; rapacity or extreme gluttony.
parole.testo: First attested in 1526 from Middle French voracité, from Latin vorācitās (whence -acity), from vorāx.

parole.significato: Dedicated or given in fulfillment of a vow or pledge.
parole.testo: From Middle French votif, from Latin vōtīvus (“votive”), from vōtum (“vow”).

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of Wallonia.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French Wallon / wallon, from Frankish *walh, from Proto-Germanic *walhaz (“foreigner”). Cognate to English Welsh/Wales, the second part of Cornwall, and first part of walnut, as well as Gaul and Wallachia.

parole.significato: Any of three freshwater dabbling ducks.
parole.testo: Early 16th century. Probably from Middle French vigeon, from Old French vigeon, vingeon (“wigeon”), from Old French vignier (“to whine or shout”) + -on (“noun suffix”).

parole.significato: Unusual and awkward in a funny, comical manner; outlandish; clownish.
parole.testo: From Middle French zani, zanni, from Italian zanni (“a kind of masked clown character”), from Zanni, a Venetian form of Giovanni. Doublet of Zanni, John, and Giovanni.

parole.significato: An animal thought to have the characteristics of a plant, later specifically an invertebrate of the (former) group Zoop…
parole.testo: From zoo- + -phyte, after Middle French zoophyte; later reinforced by scientific Latin Zoophyta.

parole.significato: A low or downcast condition; meanness of spirit; abasement; degradation.
parole.testo: From Middle English abjeccioun, from either Middle French abjection or Late Latin abiectiōn-, from Latin abiectus (“cast down”). * See abject.

parole.significato: To flee, often secretly; to steal away.
parole.testo: Either borrowed from Middle French abscondre or directly from Latin abscondō (“hide”); formed from abs, ab (“away”) + condō (“put together, store”), from con- (“together”) + *dʰeh₁- (“to put, place, set”). * Cognate with sconce (“a type of light fixture”).

parole.significato: To make clean by wiping; to wipe away.
parole.testo: From French and Middle French absterger or from Medieval Latin abstergēre (“wipe off or away”); formed from Latin abs- + tergeō (“to wipe off”).

parole.significato: The act of abstracting, separating, withdrawing, or taking away; withdrawal; the state of being taken away.
parole.testo: From Middle English abstraccyone; either from Middle French abstraction or from Medieval Latin abstrāctiō (“separation”), from Latin abstrahō (“draw away”). Equivalent to abstract + -ion.

parole.significato: That which is absurd; an absurd action; a logical contradiction.
parole.testo: First attested around 1472. From Middle English absurdite, then from either Middle French absurdité, or from Late Latin absurditas (“dissonance, incongruity”), from Latin absurdus + -itas (“quality, state, degree”). Equivalent to absurd + -ity.

parole.significato: A way or means of approaching or entering; an entrance; a passage.
parole.testo: From Middle English accesse, acces, borrowed from Middle French acces (“attack, onslaught”) or from its source Latin accessus, perfect passive participle of accēdō (“approach; accede”), from ad (“to, toward, at”) + cēdō (“move, yield”). Doublet of accessus. First attested in the early 14th century.

parole.significato: An attempt to assume or exhibit what is not natural or real; false display; artificial show.
parole.testo: From Middle French affectation and its etymon Latin affectātiōnem, from affectō (“to feign”). By surface analysis, affect + -ation.

parole.significato: A word or phrase that is created by rearranging the letters of another word or phrase.
parole.testo: Late 16th century, either from Middle French anagramme or Latin anagramma, formed on Ancient Greek ἀνά (aná, “up, back”) + γράμμα (grámma, “letter”). Analyzable as ana- (“up, back”) + -gram (“letter”).

parole.significato: The creation or formation of anagrams.
parole.testo: Either from Middle French anagrammatisme or Ancient Greek ἀναγραμματισμός (anagrammatismós).

parole.significato: The indigo shrub; or the indigo dye obtained from the plant.
parole.testo: From Middle French anil, Portuguese anil.

parole.significato: Of or relating to water.
parole.testo: Formed from Latin aqua + -ous (or from Medieval Latin aqueus), partly the analogy of Middle French aqueux (itself actually from Latin aquosus). Or based on the analogy of Latin terreus from terra.

parole.significato: Relating to Armorica; Armorican.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English Armorik, from Latin Armoricus directly or from Middle French Armorique.

parole.significato: An inflatable buoyant object, often (but not necessarily) round and flexible.
parole.testo: First use appears c. 1591, "a game played with a large, inflated leather ball" (possibly via Middle French ballon) from Italian pallone (“large ball”) from palla (“ball”), from Lombardic *palla. parole.testo: First attested in 1730. Origin uncertain, perhaps of Cornish origin (recorded as blogon c. 1450) or from Middle French bougeon, a diminutive of bouge (“club, stick”).

parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French carnage, from a Norman or Picard variant Old Northern French) of Old French charnage, from char (“flesh”), or from Vulgar Latin *carnaticum (“slaughter of animals”), itself from Latin carnem, accusative of caro (“flesh”). parole.significato: A type of Eurasian plant widely cultivated for its flowers.
parole.testo: From Middle French carnation (“flesh color, complexion”), either via Italian carnagione (“flesh color”) or directly from Late Latin carnātiō (“fleshiness”), from Latin carō (“flesh, meat”) + ātiō (“-ation”). parole.testo: From cellar + -age. In the fee sense, apparently after either Middle French celerage, celeraige, cellerage, sceleraige or Latin celērāgium, cellārāgium.

parole.significato: An underground pit where sewage is held.
parole.testo: From earlier sesspool. Origin uncertain. Perhaps from Italian cesso (“privy, a toilet”) + English pool. parole.significato: To commix.
parole.testo: From Middle English commixten, commyxten, either from Middle French commixtre or Latin commixtus, past participle of commisceō.

parole.significato: Comfort, support or sympathy.
parole.testo: From condole + -ence, or from Middle French condoléance, or formed from the root of Latin condoleō (“to sympathize”), from con- (“together, with”) and doleō (“to hurt, suffer, have pain”).

parole.significato: A form of needlework that is made by looping thread with a hooked needle.
parole.testo: From French crochet, from Middle French crochet, from Old French crochet, crokét (“curved instrument, hook”), diminutive of Old French croc (“hook”), from Old Frankish *krōk (“hook”) or from Old Norse krókr (“hook, bend, bight”), both from Proto-Germanic *krōkaz (“hook”), from Proto-Indo-European *g

parole.significato: A performer's first performance to the public, in sport, the arts or some other area.
parole.testo: Borrowed from French début, from Middle French, derivative of débuter (“to move, begin”), from dé- + but (“mark, goal”), from Old French but (“aim, goal, end, target”), from Old French butte (“mound, knoll, target”), from Frankish *but (“stump, log”), or from Old Norse bútr (“log, stump, butt”); bot

parole.significato: Of or concerning the teeth.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dental or Late Latin dentālis, from dēns (“a tooth”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: Composed of inherently different or distinct elements; incongruous.
parole.testo: First attested in 1586; either borrowed from Middle French desparat or directly from Latin disparātus, perfect passive participle of disparō (“to divide”) (see -ate (adjective-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix)), from dis- (“apart”) + parō (“to arrange”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-Europ

parole.significato: To make domestic.
parole.testo: First attested in 1620; either borrowed from Middle French domestiquer (Modern French domestiquer) or directly from Medieval Latin domesticātus, perfect passive participle of domesticō (“to domesticate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, domestic + -ate.

parole.significato: A fabric, usually of thick cotton or wool, having a dull brownish yellow, dull grey, or dun colour.
parole.testo: Probably from Middle French and Old French drap (“cloth”), either: * from Late Latin drappus (“drabcloth, kerchief; piece of cloth”), most likely from Gaulish *drappo, from Proto-Indo-European *drep- (“to scratch, tear”); or * from Frankish *drapi, *drāpi (“that which is fulled, drabcloth”), from Pr

parole.significato: To compel (a person or persons) to leave.
parole.testo: From Middle French éjecter, from Latin ēiectus, perfect passive participle of ēiciō (“to throw out”), or from ēiectō, the frequentative form of the same verb, from ē-, combining form of ex (“out”), + iaciō (“to throw”).

parole.significato: In the neighbourhood; around.

parole.significato: An officer responsible for the care and supervision of the horses of a person of rank.
parole.testo: From an alteration of earlier esquiry (through the influence of the unrelated Latin equus), from Middle French escuirie, escuerie, derivative of escuyer (“squire”), or alternatively from Medieval Latin scuria (“stable”), from Old High German scura (“barn”). Compare esquire.

parole.significato: Wild; untamed.
parole.testo: From Latin fera (“wild beast”, noun) + -al or Latin ferus (“wild; savage; cruel”, adjective) + -al. Alternatively, borrowed from Middle French féral or Late Latin ferālis.

parole.significato: To protect from danger; to secure against surprise, attack, or injury; to keep in safety; to defend.

parole.significato: Chronologically first, early; of or pertaining to the beginning, cause or origin.
parole.testo: From Middle French initial or directly from its Latin etymon initiālis (“of the beginning, incipient, initial”), from initium (“a going in, entrance”), from inīre (“to go into, enter”), from in (“in”) + ire (“to go”).

parole.significato: Something invented.

parole.significato: To spend money, time, or energy on something, especially for some benefit or purpose; used with in.

parole.significato: A short strap fastened around the leg of a bird used in falconry, to which a leash may be fastened.

parole.significato: A cheeky, impudent, or saucy person.
parole.testo: From mal- (“not, badly”) + apert (“open, revealed; direct, straightforward; clever, expert”), or from Middle French malappert, Old French mal apert (“ill-skilled”).

parole.significato: A marsh.
parole.testo: From Middle English mareys, marys, from Anglo-Norman mareis, mereis, or from Middle French mares, marest, both from Late Latin mariscus, from Proto-West Germanic *marisk (“marsh”). Doublet of marsh and morass.

parole.significato: A type of bolthead flask used in chemical distillation.
parole.testo: From New Latin matracium and its source, Middle French matheras, matraz etc., either from Middle French materas (see Etymology 1, above), with reference to its shape, or from Arabic مطرة, مطارة (“leather bottle, vase”).

parole.significato: A medicine, medication or drug.
parole.testo: From Middle English medicament, either from Middle French médicament or its etymon, Latin medicāmentum.

parole.significato: In French heraldry, a depiction of a mythological bird without beak or feet.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English [Term?], from Anglo-Norman merlet (from merle (“blackbird”) + -et (“suffix forming a noun”)), or from Middle French merlette (“little blackbird; merlette (heraldic charge)”) (from merle (“blackbird”)—formerly a feminine noun) + -ette (“diminutive suffix for a feminine noun”)

parole.significato: To make (something) moist or wet; to moisten.

parole.significato: Any of a set of signs used in early musical notation.
parole.testo: From 15th c. Middle English newme, nevme, neme; from Middle French neume, in turn from Medieval Latin neuma or pneuma, either from Ancient Greek νεῦμα (neûma, “sign”), or else a corruption of πνεῦμα (pneûma, “breath”). In the latter case a doublet of pneuma.

parole.significato: Of or related to the number ninety.

parole.significato: A novice.

parole.significato: Character typical of a prudhomme; trustworthiness, loyalty.

parole.testo: Either from Middle French escouillon (“a swab, cloth”), diminutive of escouve (“broom, twig”) from Latin scopa, or an alteration of Old French souillon (“scullion”) by influence of scullery.

parole.significato: A ruler; a carpenter's square; a measure.

parole.significato: The holder of a secular office, formally subordinate to, but de facto the power behind the throne of, the caliph.

parole.significato: Capable of being supported, upheld, maintained, or defended.

parole.significato: To violate, especially to rape.
